questions.q: DIN 69901 defines a project as an undertaking that is delimited in content, planning and time. Which further element does the definition explicitly require?
options: A separate, temporary organization created for it
A minimum contract value set by the client
A permanent line department that owns the work
At least two participating legal entities
questions.why: DIN 69901 names three delimitations (content, planning, time) and a separate, temporary organization. The temporary organization is what distinguishes a project from routine line work — no value threshold, no permanent department and no minimum number of parties appears in the definition.

questions.q: Which characteristics does the lecture list for a project?
options: Unique, because the task is novel and complex
Limited in time by a start and an end
Limited human, material and financial resources
Repeats at fixed intervals with a stable output
Project-specific organization (team)
questions.why: Uniqueness, time limitation, limited resources and a project-specific team are the four bullets on the definition slide. Repetition at fixed intervals is the opposite — that describes a process, which consists of partly repetitive operations.

questions.q: Assign each wording to the standard or body that uses it.
pairs: "a temporary organization created for the purpose of delivering one or more business products according to an agreed business case"
"a unique set of processes consisting of coordinated and controlled activities with start and finish dates"
"a series of structured tasks, activities and deliverables … temporary efforts to create value"
"undertakings that can be delimited in terms of content, planning and time … separate, temporary organization"
questions.why: PRINCE2 frames the project as a temporary organization tied to a business case; ISO 21500 speaks of a unique set of processes; PMI stresses tasks, deliverables and value creation; DIN 69901 is the German definition built on delimitation plus temporary organization.

questions.q: The magic triangle of project management puts quality in the middle. Name the three corners.
questions.why: Scope (features, functionality, performance), cost (resources, budget) and time (schedule, production rate) span the triangle; quality sits in the centre because it results from how the three are balanced.

questions.q: What distinguishes a process from a project in the lecture's definition?
options: A process has a defined start event (input) and result (output) and consists of partly repetitive operations
A process is always longer than a project
A process needs no task owners, only material resources
A process creates value only for the company itself, never for customers
questions.why: The process definition centres on input → output and on repetition; a project is by definition unique and non-repetitive. Duration is irrelevant, processes explicitly do have task owners, and the definition says a process "serves to create value for customers".

questions.q: What does the UK output-per-hour data (1970–2020) shown in the lecture say about the construction industry?
options: There has been nearly no increase in productivity over the last 50 years
Productivity roughly doubled every decade
Productivity fell sharply until 1990 and then recovered fully
Construction outperformed the rest of the market sector throughout
questions.why: The slide's punchline is that construction productivity has stagnated for five decades while the wider market sector grew — this stagnation is the motivation for the digitalisation and industrialisation push discussed in Lecture 5.

questions.q: Which challenges does the lecture name as the construction industry's biggest?
options: Lack of sustainability — 38 % of global carbon emissions (cradle to grave)
Lack of efficiency — low productivity, no disruptive innovation
Lack of commitments — exploding costs and delays
Lack of qualified personnel
Lack of demand — order books shrinking worldwide
questions.why: Sustainability, efficiency, commitment and resources (personnel) are the four challenges on the ICoM slide, with 33.5 % of German companies reporting problems finding qualified staff. Demand is not the problem — the sector's issue is delivering, not selling.

questions.q: The Chinese contractor COVEC won the A2 Express Highway in Poland at roughly €420 m while the government had estimated about €1 bn, and the contract later collapsed. Which lesson does the case illustrate best?
options: A price far below the client's own estimate is a warning sign, not a competitive advantage
Foreign contractors are legally barred from EU infrastructure markets
Fixed-price contracts always protect the client from cost increases
Football tournaments are unsuitable as project deadlines
questions.why: COVEC underbid by roughly 60 %, then discovered that Polish wages, materials and standards made the price unachievable. The client did not benefit — the works stopped, both sides claimed compensation, and the dispute only settled in 2017. The other options are not what the case shows.

questions.q: Which reasons for the COVEC project failure does the lecture list?
options: The contractor was not used to European standards
Failure to provide financial records
Poorly organized leadership
Underestimated cost of Polish wages and materials
Polish subcontractors refused cooperation and materials
The route had to be rebuilt after a design error by the Polish road agency
questions.why: The slide lists unfamiliar standards, missing financial records, poor leadership, underestimated local costs, refusing subcontractors, the belief that the Chinese state would cover losses, and a communication gap due to cultural differences. A design error by the client is not among them.

questions.q: Why did the STRABAG–Aveng joint venture terminate the Mtentu Bridge contract in South Africa in 2019?
options: Risk to the safety and wellbeing of its personnel after protests and threats
The client became insolvent
The design was found to be structurally impossible
Currency restrictions blocked all payments
questions.why: Villagers protested over broken promises of employment and workers and management were threatened, including with assault rifles — a social/political risk, not a technical or financial one. The replacement contract went to a Chinese–South African JV at roughly twice the original price.

questions.q: The new San Giorgio Bridge in Genoa was completed in 15 months. Which principles make up the "Genova Model"?
options: Collaboration — working together towards the same objective
Transparency — opened to the public
Teamwork throughout the whole supply chain
Strict separation of designer and contractor to avoid liability
Penalty-driven contracting with maximum risk transfer
questions.why: Collaboration, transparency and supply-chain-wide teamwork are the three pillars of the Genova Model. It is the deliberate counter-example to adversarial, penalty-driven set-ups — separation and maximum risk transfer are exactly what it avoids.

questions.q: Contrast Ponte Morandi (2018) with the New San Giorgio Bridge (2020) — what happened, and why is the pair used in the lecture?
questions.answer:
Ponte Morandi, August 2018: a section collapsed during a summer storm; 43 people killed, 600 left homeless. It raised open questions on design issues, material failures and a construction authority that foresaw no problems; trials on operators and maintenance units are still ongoing.

New San Giorgio Bridge, August 2020: 1,100 m long, ~€200 m, built 24/7 and completed within 15 months without construction ever stopping — presented as a masterpiece of large-scale infrastructure management under the "Genova Model".

The pair shows both sides of the same coin: neglected maintenance and unclear responsibility destroy a structure, while collaboration, transparency and teamwork can deliver a replacement at extraordinary speed.
questions.why: The lecture uses failure and success on the same site to argue that management culture — not technology — decides the outcome.

questions.q: Match each landmark project to the delay reported in the lecture.
questions.why: All three are used to show that deadline and budget risk are structural, not exotic. Sydney is the extreme on cost (14.6×), the Elbphilharmonie the shortest delay of the three, and BER matches Sydney's ten years while staying below it on the cost multiple.

questions.q: What is the term for employees sent from Germany or another industrialized country to work on a foreign project site?
questions.why: Expatriates are the posted staff from the home country. They sit alongside locals (host-country employees) and third country nationals (TCNs) — the three groups whose mix defines the personnel logistics of an international site.

questions.q: On an international site, what is the abbreviation TCN short for?
questions.why: TCNs are employees from a country that is neither the contractor's home country nor the host country. Recruiting them means planning departure formalities such as visas and, where needed, on-site training.

questions.q: Which qualities should an expatriate bring, according to the selection slide?
questions.answer:
• Above-average experience
  • Highly qualified professionally
  • Ready to adapt / adaptable
  • Reliable
  • Foreign language skills
  • Resilient and healthy
  • Strengthened character

Note the balance: only two of the seven are technical. The rest are personality and health — the lecture's point is that posting abroad fails on people, not on engineering.
questions.why: The exam-relevant "You should know" list explicitly asks why expatriates are needed and which skills they should have.

questions.q: Sort each statement into the staffing approach it describes.
items: Employees and PM techniques come from the home country
Home country remains the main market
Usually no consideration of foreign specifics
Host country is the focus of corporate efforts
Goal: highest possible integration into the foreign market
High autonomy of the foreign organization
Company activities are aligned with the global market
questions.why: Ethnocentric = monoculture / home-country orientation, polycentric = multiculture / host-country orientation, geocentric = mixed culture / world-market orientation. Reading the orientation in each statement is the fastest way to place it.

questions.q: Which is a disadvantage of the ethnocentric approach?
options: Potential for conflict due to culturally different views and attitudes
Communication problems between foreign branch and head office
Often low know-how transfer
Very complex communication structures
questions.why: Ethnocentric staffing risks cultural conflict, preferential treatment of parent-company staff and high posting costs. The other three are the drawbacks of the other approaches: communication problems and low know-how transfer belong to polycentric, complex communication structures to geocentric.

questions.q: A contractor wants to enter a large but unfamiliar market permanently, wants low personnel costs and needs staff who understand the local language and business customs. Which staffing approach fits?
options: Polycentric
Ethnocentric
Geocentric
None — this always requires posting expatriates
questions.why: Low personnel costs plus language, market and cultural experience of employees are exactly the listed advantages of the polycentric approach. Ethnocentric would import home-country staff at high posting cost; geocentric aims at a global market position rather than one market.

questions.q: Which pair of advantages does the lecture give for the geocentric approach?
options: Utilization of worldwide employee potential and high know-how transfer
Low personnel costs and easy communication
Uniform company policy and familiar instruments
Complete independence of the foreign organization
questions.why: Geocentric staffing draws on the global talent pool and moves know-how across borders — at the price of high posting costs and very complex communication structures. Low personnel costs belong to polycentric, uniform policy and familiar instruments to ethnocentric.

questions.q: Match each organizational form of an international project to its defining feature.
pairs: The project manager mediates between departments and has no direct authority to issue directives
Two equivalent lines of instruction; each employee reports to a department head and to the project manager
All authority to issue directives and make decisions lies with the project manager; staff are outsourced from business units
questions.why: The three forms are a ladder of project-manager power: none (influence), shared (matrix), full (autonomous). The autonomous form is described as very widespread in the international project business precisely because distance makes divided authority unworkable.

questions.q: Which organizational form does the lecture call "very widespread in the international project business"?
options: Autonomous organization
Influence organization
Matrix organization
Line organization without a project manager
questions.why: Autonomous organization gives the PM exclusive responsibility and full flexibility — indispensable when the site is thousands of kilometres from head office. The influence form is described as rather for small projects, the matrix form as frequent when all organizational areas of the company are affected.

questions.q: Sort each feature into "Traditional / direct export" foreign construction or "Area business" (Flächengeschäft).
items: Building in developing and emerging countries without an efficient construction industry of their own
Export of construction and design services
Building in industrialized countries with their own efficient construction industry
Services provided by national subsidiaries and associated companies
questions.why: Traditional foreign construction is project-by-project export into markets that lack a local industry — capital-intensive, staff-intensive, often donor-financed. Area business is a permanent corporate presence via subsidiaries in developed markets, needing far fewer posted executives.

questions.q: Besides traditional foreign construction and area business, the lecture names a third field of activity. Which one?
options: Engineering services — consulting and planning in developing, emerging and industrialized countries (services export)
Property speculation in host countries
Operation of national building authorities
Sale of construction machinery
questions.why: Engineering services cover consulting and planning across all country groups and are exported as a service, without the contractor building anything itself.

questions.q: Complete the stakeholder definitions.
questions.text: DIN 69901-5 defines project stakeholders as all participants and interested parties whose {{}} are directly or indirectly affected by the course or outcome of the project. The corresponding {{}} analysis examines stakeholders in terms of their influence on the project and their attitude — positive or negative — towards it.
questions.why: The two halves matter together: the definition says who counts as a stakeholder (anyone whose interests are affected), and the stakeholder analysis says what you do with the list — plot influence against attitude, then act accordingly.

questions.q: According to the lecture's definition, a stakeholder is a person, group or organization that …
options: is actively involved in the project
is influenced by the course or outcome of the project
can influence the course of the project or the project result
holds a share of the contract sum
has signed a contract with the employer
questions.why: Involvement, being influenced, or being able to influence — any one of the three is enough. A financial share or a contract is not required, which is why protesting villagers (Mtentu) or the general public count as stakeholders. PRINCE2 goes further still and includes those who merely feel influenced.

questions.q: In the international project structure according to FIDIC, what is the special position of the "Engineer"?
options: Competent representative of the employer who organizes and controls technical, legal and economic issues
The design office of the contractor
An independent state authority that grants building permits
The financing institution's local agent
questions.why: The Engineer reflects the Anglo-Saxon view: an appointee of the employer who administers the contract technically, legally and economically. It is not a state body, not the contractor's designer and not the financier's agent — those are the separate roles of public authorities, the designer and the financier in the same diagram.

questions.q: What is a nominated subcontractor in the FIDIC structure?
options: A subcontractor selected by the employer and/or engineer rather than by the contractor
A subcontractor that has been pre-qualified by the local chamber of commerce
The largest subcontractor by contract value
A subcontractor working without a written contract
questions.why: The word "nominated" refers to who chooses: the employer or engineer picks the firm, while an ordinary subcontractor is selected by the contractor and renders its own services. That distinction matters because it shifts responsibility for the choice away from the contractor.

questions.q: What is the role of the Resident Engineer?
options: The Engineer's representative on site, monitoring the works as the builder's construction manager
The contractor's site manager
A specialist engineer commissioned by the employer for geotechnics
The employer's legal counsel on site
questions.why: "Resident" means permanently on the site — the Engineer's representative there. Specialist engineers such as geotechnical engineers or quantity surveyors are the separate consultants box in the same diagram, commissioned by the Engineer.

questions.q: Match the German construction terms to the English FIDIC terms taught in the lecture.
questions.why: These are the bold, FIDIC-defined terms. Getting them wrong in a notice or a claim is exactly the "lost in translation" problem the guest lecture warns about — the lecturer's rule is: English is the lingua franca, so learn and use the right technical terms.

questions.q: In the extended FIDIC diagram the financier is linked to the project by which flow?
options: Cash flow to the employer, who pays the contractor
A construction contract directly with the contractor
Supervision and instruction authority over the engineer
A guarantee issued to the subcontractors
questions.why: Financing institutions such as the World Bank or KfW provide the cash flow but stay outside the contractual chain — the construction contract runs between employer and contractor only. Their influence is exercised through funding conditions, not through instructions.

questions.q: In the classic German project structure, what is the "planner contract" (Architekten-/Ingenieurvertrag) between client and designer supposed to settle?
options: The powers of the owner's construction manager and which powers of instruction the owner's representatives have towards the contractor
The contractor's warranty periods
The subcontractor payment schedule
The insurance premiums for the works
questions.why: The footnote on the slide is explicit: the planner contract must be adapted per project so that it regulates the owner's construction manager's powers and the instruction rights towards the contractor. The construction contract itself (per BGB and/or VOB) covers warranties and payment.

questions.q: Recall the "You should know" list of Lecture 1.
questions.answer:
• How a construction project is defined
  • The characteristics and challenges of international construction projects
  • Common mistakes in international projects, do's and don'ts
  • Some of the largest construction companies in Germany and worldwide
  • Why we need expatriates and which skills they should have
  • Where you get your personnel from, and on site
  • The approaches to staffing
  • The organizational forms of international projects and which to choose
  • The fields of activity of German foreign construction
  • What stakeholders are and how to meet them
  • The international structure according to FIDIC
questions.why: This list is the stated exam scope for Lecture 1 and is repeated verbatim in the Lecture 7 recapitulation.

questions.q: A project development process can start from three constellations. Which set does the lecture name?
options: Location seeks capital and project idea · Project seeks location and capital · Capital seeks location and project idea
Client seeks contractor · Contractor seeks client · Bank seeks both
Design seeks approval · Approval seeks design · Site seeks approval
Tender seeks bidder · Bidder seeks tender · Engineer seeks tender
questions.why: The triangle is location – capital – project idea; whichever two you already have, you are looking for the third. All three paths then converge on the same sequence: rough description, feasibility analysis, project concretization.

questions.q: Which analyses belong to the feasibility analysis in the project development process?
options: Market analysis
Location analysis
Analysis of the utilization concept
Competition analysis
Risk analysis
Defects liability analysis
questions.why: Market, location, utilization concept, competition and risk are the five columns of the feasibility analysis, capped by a profitability and yield analysis. Defects liability is a contractual matter that only arises long after the realization decision.

questions.q: Which two approaches are named for the simple project development calculation at concept stage?
questions.why: The frontdoor approach starts from costs and derives the rent/price needed to make them work; the backdoor approach starts from the achievable rent/price and derives the cost budget that is affordable. Both appear at the concept stage, before the feasibility analysis.

questions.q: Match each financing-model abbreviation to what it stands for.
questions.why: Read the letters literally. The presence or absence of the final T is the key commercial question: with transfer the asset returns to the public side after the concession, without it (BOO) the operator keeps it permanently.

questions.q: A government wants a private consortium to build and run a toll road for 30 years, after which ownership passes to the state. Which model is that?
options: BOT — Build-Operate-Transfer
BOO — Build-Own-Operate
ROT — Renovate-Own-Transfer
EXW — Ex Works
questions.why: Build, operate for the concession period, then transfer: BOT. BOO would leave the road permanently with the consortium, ROT applies to an existing asset that is refurbished rather than newly built, and EXW is an Incoterm, not a financing model.

questions.q: Complete the guarantee structure for a national construction project.
questions.text: The construction company is the {{}} and owes performance of the contract (primary liability). The bank acts as {{}} and enters into a guarantee contract, taking on secondary liability. The builder or client is the {{}}, who owes the remuneration.
questions.why: The bank's liability is secondary: it only steps in if the contractor (the debtor with primary liability) fails to perform. Naming the roles correctly is what makes the difference between a guarantee and a mere comfort letter.

questions.q: Match each guarantee to what it secures.
pairs: That the bidder stands by its offer and will sign if awarded
Repayment of money the client paid before any work was done
Proper, contract-compliant execution of the works
Remedy of defects after taking over, during the notification period
The customs obligations of the contractor towards the host country's authorities
questions.why: The guarantees follow the project timeline: bid → advance payment → execution → defects period, with the customs guarantee running alongside towards a different beneficiary (the host state, not the client).

questions.q: What does the Hermes cover protect a German construction company against?
options: Losses from economic and political risks in export transactions
Site accidents and personal injury on the construction site
Defects in the contractor's own design work
Exchange-rate movements between order and delivery
questions.why: Hermes cover is a federal export credit guarantee against economic and political risk — the Federal Republic of Germany stands behind it, with Euler Hermes AG acting as the government's mandatary. Site accidents and design defects are matters for ordinary liability insurance.

questions.q: Which company handles the German export credit guarantees (Hermes cover) and UFK guarantees on behalf of the Federal Republic of Germany?
questions.why: Euler Hermes acts as the Federal Government's mandatary — it administers the scheme but the risk is carried by the state, which is why decisions above €10 m go to the Interministerial Committee (IMA).

questions.q: Match each institution to its role in financing projects in Africa.
pairs: Loans and grants for infrastructure, education, health and poverty reduction, through sub-organizations such as IDA and IFC
Lends to countries with balance-of-payments difficulties — no direct project financing
German loans, subsidies and guarantees for infrastructure projects such as roads, bridges and energy supply
Receives BMZ funds and works on urban development and sustainable building — but awards no loans
Decides on the allocation of German development funds and passes them to KfW and GIZ
Primarily finances state projects and invests in the infrastructure sector
questions.why: Two traps are worth memorising: the IMF does not finance projects (it supports balance of payments), and GIZ does not award loans (it implements, KfW lends). BMZ is the ministry that decides, KfW and GIZ are the implementing arms.

questions.q: Which of these is listed as a commercial lender (covered by export insurance) rather than a classic funder?
options: China Export-Import Bank
World Bank
African Development Bank
Islamic Development Bank
questions.why: The classic funders are the multilateral and development banks (World Bank, KfW, AfDB, AFD, AIIB, IsDB). The commercial-lender column lists Euler Hermes, Delcredere Ducroire, the OPEC Fund and the China Export-Import Bank, all backed by export insurance from an export credit agency.

questions.q: Complete the definition of export from the guest lecture.
questions.text: Export in foreign trade refers to the {{}} sale of goods or services from the domestic market to foreign countries. The opposite of this is {{}}.
questions.why: The starting problem of export finance follows straight from this: the exporter delivers or invests across a border and must be sure the payment from the other side is actually secured.

questions.q: Put the four stages of an export project development in order.
items: Initiation / preparation — client acquisition, project definition, studies, local legal and permit review
Negotiation — technical specifications, export contract, prices and quantities, supply chain, logistics and insurance
Financing — production financing for the exporter, investment financing for the importer, structuring of buyer's or supplier's credit, risk coverage
Implementation / financing period — production, logistics, construction and commissioning, payment processing, repayments and reporting
questions.why: The order matters commercially: cover must be applied for before the risk starts, so the financing questions have to be settled in stage 3, not once execution has begun in stage 4.

questions.q: What is an Export Credit Agency (ECA)?
options: A private or government-related institution acting between national governments and exporters, providing export insurance cover and financial guarantees
A commercial bank specialising in trade loans to importers
A UN body that grants development aid
An arbitration institution for cross-border trade disputes
questions.why: ECAs are state-backed instruments of export promotion — intermediaries, not lenders. Crucially they are commercial support tools and therefore apply exclusively to commercial financings, not to development aid.

questions.q: Which reasons for involving an ECA does the guest lecture give?
options: The borrower's creditworthiness is not sufficient for an unsecured loan
The requested loan tenor is commercially not feasible
There is a long lead time before the first repayment, which banks shy away from
An ECA-covered tranche is eligible as cover pool, enabling refinancing via the capital market
The ECA takes over project management from the exporter
questions.why: All four commercial reasons concern bankability: credit standing, tenor, lead time and refinancing. An ECA never manages the project — it only insures the risk, and even then never fully (see the mandatory retainer).

questions.q: Put the ECA application process (identical across the OECD) into the right order.
items: Submission of application by the exporter and, if applicable, the bank
Review process by the ECA; environmental and social assessment if applicable
Review by the decision committee (IMA) for applications above €10 m — unanimous decision required
Cover decision — preliminary cover commitment letter, possibly with conditions or collateral requirements
Notification post signing — ECA is informed of contract signing and fulfilment of requirements
Notification of final cover — cover document and premium invoice issued
Payment of the premium, thereby activating the cover
questions.why: Two thresholds structure the process: the ECA decides alone below €5 m without special restrictions, while anything above €10 m must go to the Interministerial Committee and needs unanimity. The cover is only effective once the premium is paid — until then it is in pending ineffectiveness.

questions.q: Above which transaction value must an ECA application be submitted to the Interministerial Committee (IMA)?
options: €10 million
€5 million
€100 million
questions.why: Above €10 m the IMA decides, and its decision must be unanimous. The €5 m figure is the other threshold on the slide: below it, and absent special restrictions, the ECA reviews and decides on its own.

questions.q: Match each ECA cover type to the risk it addresses.
pairs: Unjustified calling of the advance payment guarantee by the buyer
Goods are not completed because the buyer becomes insolvent or political reasons make delivery impossible
Loss of receivables / non-payment for economic or political reasons
Up to 80 % relief of credit lines for required contract guarantees
questions.why: The four covers map onto the timeline: before delivery (bonds and manufacturing), after delivery (supplier credit), and running throughout (performance bond relief, which frees the exporter's bank credit lines rather than insuring a loss).

questions.q: Complete the basic principles of ECA coverage.
questions.text: A mandatory retainer of 5–{{}} % applies for economic risks and {{}} % for political risks. The application for coverage must be submitted strictly {{}} the start of the risk.
questions.why: The retainer is deliberate: leaving 5–15 % of the economic risk with the exporter keeps its incentive to choose sound buyers. And an application filed after the risk has started is worthless — no cover can be granted retroactively.

questions.q: Match each ECA-covered financing structure to its defining feature.
pairs: The bank lends directly to the buyer / borrower abroad
The exporter itself acts as indirect financier by granting the buyer payment terms
Used when the creditworthiness of the buyer alone is insufficient
questions.why: The question in every structure is who carries the receivable. In a buyer credit it is the bank; in a supplier credit it stays with the exporter (hence supplier credit cover); onlending inserts a stronger intermediate borrower when the buyer alone is not bankable. A further special case is when buyer and borrower are simply not the same entity.

questions.q: Which basic conditions does the OECD Consensus set for export projects with a tenor over two years?
options: Loan amount max. 85 % of the contract value (15 % advance and interim payment)
Local costs up to 70 % of the contract value for projects in the green category
At least one payment per year, in connection with interest payment
Loan term max. 18 years, up to 22 years for green-category projects
A minimum interest rate of 5 % on all covered tranches
questions.why: 85 % / 15 %, local costs, annual payment and the 18- or 22-year tenor are the stated conditions. There is no fixed minimum interest rate — the interest side is instead handled by the separate CIRR fixed interest rate programme.

questions.q: Since April 2023 every cover application is classified into three categories. Sort these.
items: Bioenergy, green hydrogen, district heating and cooling networks
Simplified and more attractive cover conditions; longer tenors and premium discount
No significant contribution to the Paris climate goals, but not in contradiction to the 1.5-degree target
Conditions remain unchanged; also covers decommissioning of fossil energy infrastructure
Coal-fired power plants and oil extraction
Exclusion from cover — no export credit or investment guarantees
questions.why: The traffic-light logic ties export promotion to the 1.5-degree target: green is rewarded (better terms, up to 22 years, 70 % local costs), white is neutral, red is excluded outright. Note that converting fossil infrastructure to non-fossil use falls under white, not red.

questions.q: Under the OECD sustainable lending principles, what happens when a lower-income country is under an ongoing IMF or World Bank programme?
options: Commercial borrowing is limited via a Commercial Lending Window, and pending ECA-covered financings must be reported to the IMF / World Bank
All ECA cover is automatically granted at reduced premiums
The country is excluded from any form of financing
Only grants are permitted, and repayment is waived
questions.why: The aim is to prevent renewed over-indebtedness of HIPC and MDRI countries. Each country gets a Commercial Lending Window reviewed annually against budget consolidation progress; development loans should carry a grant element of up to 35 %, and without approval the cover may not legally be granted.

questions.q: Match the abbreviations from the sustainable lending slide.
pairs: Heavily Indebted Poor Countries Initiative for Debt Relief
Debt Service Suspension Initiative (World Bank and G20)
questions.why: All three are debt-relief mechanisms. The lecture's point is that relief alone did not fix the structural problems, which is why lending practice itself had to be restricted afterwards.

questions.q: Sort each characteristic into ECA cover or PRI (political risk insurance).
items: Pre-calculated risk premium, payable before the insurance takes effect, transparent premium scheme
Complex application process lasting at least three months
95 % of political and commercial risk, long tenors possible
180 days waiting period in a claim event; often a political solution is sought
Annual premia subject to fluctuation, risk-adjusted market prices, usually more expensive
Application submitted directly or via bank — fast and efficient
50–100 % of the commercial risk; several insurers may have to be bundled via a broker
Compensation after 120–180 days, usually an efficient review procedure
questions.why: The trade-off is speed and flexibility against price and depth of cover: PRI is quick and adaptable but dearer and shallower, ECA is slow and bureaucratic but cheap, deep (95 %) and long. That is why PRI is presented as the alternative when ECA cover is unavailable.

questions.q: Which starting points and goals does the lecture place around "strategic procurement"?
options: Volume concentration
Product improvement
Process improvement
Customer relationship
Global procurement
Market / price evaluations
Reduction of the number of building permits
questions.why: The six fields around strategic procurement are volume concentration, product improvement, process improvement, customer relationship, global procurement and market/price evaluations. Building permits are a matter of public law, not procurement strategy.

questions.q: Put the eight steps of the procurement process into the right order.
items: Develop general product and supplier information
questions.why: Steps 1–4 are the strategy half (what do we need, what can the market give, what is our plan) and steps 5–8 the tactical half (choose, negotiate, integrate, evaluate). The process ends in continuous evaluation, so it is a loop rather than a straight line.

questions.q: In the make-or-buy matrix, a service with high internal complexity (significant internal resources or specialised know-how) and low external complexity (easy market access, many suppliers, low risk) points to which strategy?
options: Make
Spontaneous procurement
Capital participations
Long-term framework contract
questions.why: High internal complexity means you hold the know-how, low external complexity means the market offers no advantage — so you keep it in house. The opposite corner (low internal, high external) leads to capital participations, while low/low is spontaneous procurement.

questions.q: Which questions does the lecture list as internal influence factors in the make-or-buy decision?
options: Does the service have a high strategic importance (differentiation potential, performance on the critical path)?
Are the technical know-how and capital available?
Are these services available on the procurement market, and is there a suitable subcontractor?
What are the advantages of outsourcing in terms of price, quality, flexibility and reliability?
questions.why: Strategic importance and available know-how/capital are internal. Market availability and the outsourcing advantages are the external influence factors — the distinction matters because internal factors are the ones you can change over time.

questions.q: The lecture shows an increasing degree of standardization. Which sequence does it follow?
options: Repeated use of components/methods/processes → prefabrication on or off site → modularization of large units
Modularization → prefabrication → repeated use of components
Prefabrication → repeated use of components → single-piece production
Global sourcing → local sourcing → national sourcing
questions.why: Standardization deepens from simply reusing the same components and processes, through prefabrication, to modularizing whole large units. The stated goals stay the same throughout: improved productivity and quality, reduced costs and construction time.

questions.q: Sort each statement into the sourcing strategy it describes.
items: Purchasing from suppliers in the immediate vicinity of the construction site
Low logistical risk potential, low communication and order-processing costs
Sources of supply in your own country
Price reduction by expanding the number of possible procurement sources
Cost advantages from lower wages, taxes, energy and raw materials
Political, cultural, legal and tax risks
Logistical uncertainty that correlates with the length of the transport routes
questions.why: The three strategies trade cost against risk. Local sourcing minimises logistics risk but limits the supplier pool; global sourcing buys the lowest price but imports political, legal and transport risk — and, as the slide notes critically, often lower environmental standards.

questions.q: Match each procurement financing instrument to its description.
pairs: A credit relationship arising because the customer does not pay the supplier immediately — convenient debt financing with no interest, but the cost of forgoing the cash discount
A security under strict legal rules that can be passed on to third parties as a means of payment; extends the customer's payment period to up to 180 days
A rental agreement terminable by both parties at short notice — useful life shorter than technical life, e.g. renting equipment for the construction period
A lease agreement not terminable for a fixed period, with rates covering acquisition, ancillary and financing costs
questions.why: The pairs split cleanly: the first two are ways of paying later, the second two are ways of using an asset without buying it. Operate versus finance leasing turns on cancellability and on whether the rates amortise the asset.

questions.q: Sort these into advantages and disadvantages of central procurement.
items: Higher demand and negotiating power towards suppliers, hence better prices
Uniform appearance, reducing suppliers' market-segmentation efforts
Better enforceability of strategic decisions such as framework agreements
Development of special knowledge about materials of complex trades
Bureaucratization tendencies — cumbersome and less flexible
Remote from operations and market, so low employee satisfaction and motivation
questions.why: Centralisation buys bargaining power, consistency and compliance; it pays with rigidity and distance from the site. The lead-buyer system is presented as the compromise between the central and decentralized poles.

questions.q: The lecture splits construction-project logistics into two kinds of "logistic goods". Which?
options: Personnel logistics and material/equipment logistics
Inbound logistics and outbound logistics
Local logistics and global logistics
Approved and unapproved material
questions.why: Employees (expatriates, TCNs, locals) and material/equipment (from Germany, from third countries, from the local market) are the two flows onto the site — the same three-source pattern applies to both, which is why the lecture draws them as mirror images.

questions.q: Put the logistics process chain into order, from demand to arrival on site.
items: Construction site: determine demand qualitatively and quantitatively
Building consultant / Engineer: approve material (approval procedure)
Purchaser of the construction company: order material
Freight forwarder: organize transport and prepare material for transport
Construction site: receive and store material
questions.why: The approval step is the one that is easy to forget and expensive to skip — only material not subject to an approval procedure (e.g. site equipment) bypasses the Engineer. Information flows back up the chain while material flows down it.

questions.q: Match each transport mode to its profile in the lecture's comparison.
pairs: Low transport speed, fixed routes and low departure density, but no weight or volume limitation
Average speed, spatially and temporally very flexible, with weight and volume limitation
Average speed, spatially and temporally limited flexibility, weight and volume limitation
High transport speed and a tightly woven network with high departure density, but weight and volume limitation and possible delays with customs clearance in the host country
questions.why: The decisive contrast is between the ship (slow but unlimited in size — the only option for heavy plant) and air freight (fast but capped in weight and exposed to customs delays). Stress on conventional packaging is high by ship and medium by road and rail; containers keep it low everywhere.

questions.q: For a site in the Asian/Arab region, order the transport modes by how long before the provision date the goods must leave — longest lead time first.
items: Ship — up to 30 days before the provision date
Truck — up to 20 days before the provision date
Air freight — up to 4 days before the provision date
Transport by luggage — up to 1 day before the provision date
questions.why: The 30 / 20 / 4 / 1 ladder is also a cost ladder in reverse: the later you can still decide, the more expensive the mode. This is exactly why spare-parts strategy matters — an unplanned part may have to fly.

questions.q: The lecture compares an extensive spare parts warehouse (option 1) with quick purchase after demand determination (option 2). What does it recommend?
options: Combine both — option 1 in the first phase, option 2 in the second
Always option 1, because availability outweighs capital cost
Always option 2, because capital commitment must be avoided
Neither — spare parts should be produced on site
questions.why: Option 1 guarantees availability but ties up a lot of capital for a long time; option 2 buys only what is needed but at high per-part purchase and transport cost. The optimum is a stocked start followed by demand-driven purchasing, optionally outsourced as consignment stock.

questions.q: What is the term for goods that are owned by a supplier but stored at the customer's premises?
questions.why: Consignment stock is the outsourcing answer to the spare-parts dilemma: the parts are physically available on site, but the capital stays with the supplier until they are drawn.

questions.q: Which statements about Incoterms are correct?
options: They are trade clauses for contracting in international trade in goods
They define the responsibilities of buyers and sellers and allocate costs and risks
They are voluntarily integrable into a contract
The rulebook distinguishes 11 trading conditions
They automatically apply to every cross-border contract by law
questions.why: Incoterms are a voluntary rulebook of 11 clauses, not law — they only bind the parties if the contract incorporates them. Their job is the allocation of cost and risk at each point of the transport chain.

questions.q: Build up the logistics price from the works to the destination site — put the price stages in the order in which costs are added.
items: EXW price setting — purchase price ex works
FAS price setting — after loading in works and transport to the quay in the port of shipment, plus export costs
FOB price setting — after loading on board
CFR price setting — after sea freight to the port of destination
CIF price setting — after marine insurance
DEQ price setting — after unloading in the port of destination
DDP price setting — after import costs and transport from quay to the construction site
questions.why: Each step adds one block of cost, so the abbreviations are really a running total. Remember the two smallest jumps: FOB adds only the loading on board over FAS, and CIF adds only the marine insurance over CFR.

questions.q: Match each Incoterm to its meaning.
pairs: Free alongside ship … port of shipment
Delivered to board … port of shipment
Costs and sea freight paid to … port of destination
Costs, insurance and sea freight paid to … port of destination
Delivered carriage paid, duty paid … place of destination
questions.why: The letters encode how far the seller carries the goods and the cost. Note that FAS, FOB, CFR, CIF and DEQ are ship clauses — their use requires a ship transport, so they cannot be applied to a purely overland delivery.

questions.q: A contractor wants the supplier to bear every cost and formality up to the construction site in Nairobi, including import duty. Which clause should the contract use?
options: DDP — delivered carriage paid, duty paid
DDU — delivered carriage paid, duty unpaid
CIF — costs, insurance and freight paid to the port of destination
EXW — ex works
questions.why: DDP is the maximum-obligation clause for the seller: everything up to and including import duty at the named place. DDU stops just short of the duty, CIF stops at the port of destination, and EXW is the opposite extreme — the buyer collects at the factory gate.

questions.q: Recall the "You should know" list of Lecture 2.
questions.answer:
• Possible investment strategies for projects abroad
  • Stakeholders in project financing
  • Guarantees in international projects
  • The Hermes cover and what it is for
  • Procurement strategies
  • Procurement goals
  • The different resources to procure and how to get them to the project
  • Transport systems and Incoterms
questions.why: This is the stated exam scope for Lecture 2; the guest lecture on export finance (exficon) is explicitly exam-relevant on top of it.

questions.q: Match each definition of culture to its author.
pairs: "Culture is the collective programming of the mind that distinguishes members of one group or category of people from another."
"Culture is the way human societies find solutions to problems."
"Culture is a universal, but for a nation, society, organization and group very specific orientation system … it influences perception, thinking, values and actions."
questions.why: Three angles on the same phenomenon: Hofstede sees culture as mental programming (hence measurable dimensions), Trompenaars as problem-solving, Thomas as an orientation system that defines membership.

questions.q: Complete Hofstede's definition: "Culture is the collective … of the mind that distinguishes members of one group from another."
questions.why: "Collective programming of the mind" is the phrase to remember — it implies culture is learned and shared, not innate or individual, which is what makes cultural dimensions comparable across countries.

questions.q: Sort each element into the visible or the invisible part of the culture iceberg.
buckets: Invisible to people from other cultures (the WHY)
questions.why: The visible tip is behaviour and customs — the how. Below the waterline sit attitudes, beliefs and, deepest of all, basic values and assumptions — the why. Conflicts almost always come from the invisible part, which is why they feel inexplicable to the other side.

questions.q: In Osgood's model of cultural levels, what is the difference between percepta and concepta?
options: Percepta are the descriptive concept — results of behaviour and behaviour itself; concepta are the explicative concept — the cause of behaviour
Percepta are individual, concepta are collective
Percepta are modern, concepta are traditional
Percepta are verbal, concepta are non-verbal
questions.why: Percepta (descriptive) split into material culture — fashion, architecture, art — and social culture — customs, mores, rituals. Concepta (explicative) is mental culture: values, norms and attitudes, i.e. the cause of the behaviour you observe.

questions.q: Order Schein's cultural levels from the most visible to the least visible.
items: Symbol system — language, rituals, clothes, manners (visible, but in need of interpretation)
Norms and standards — maxims, "ideologies", code of conduct, prohibitions (partly visible, partly unconscious)
Underlying assumptions — about the environment, truth, the essence of human beings, human actions and relations (invisible, mostly unconscious)
questions.why: Schein's three levels parallel the iceberg: what you can see needs interpreting, what is half-visible is normative, and the deepest layer is unconscious. Note that the visible symbol system is not self-explanatory — misreading it is the classic expatriate error.

questions.q: Sort each behaviour into Lewis's three culture types.
items: Does one thing at a time, plans ahead step by step
Talks half the time; confronts with logic
Does several things at once, plans grand outline only
Talks most of the time, often interrupts, displays feelings
Flexible truth; seeks out the key person
Listens most of the time and reacts to the partner's action
Never confronts; must not lose face
Diplomacy over truth; statements are promises
questions.why: Linear-active is task-oriented and sequential, multi-active relationship-oriented and simultaneous, reactive listening-oriented and harmony-seeking. The lecture stresses that these are a spectrum, not boxes — real people and countries sit between the poles.

questions.q: Match each Lewis culture type to its summary description.
pairs: Task-oriented, highly organised planners who prefer getting things done one task at a time in a planned sequence; arguments are made with logic and rules are to be followed
Emotional, loquacious and impulsive, seeing family, feelings and relationships ahead of following an agenda; comfortable doing many things at the same time
Polite, attentive listeners who rarely initiate action or discussion but react to it and form their own opinion; harmony and avoiding embarrassment are core
questions.why: Each type also handles the social/professional boundary differently: linear-active separates them, multi-active interweaves them, reactive connects them — a practical predictor of how business dinners and small talk will go.

questions.q: In a meeting your counterpart listens without interrupting, gives no direct answer, avoids any open contradiction and says "we will study this carefully". Which Lewis type does this behaviour suggest, and what follows for you?
options: Reactive — expect indirect signals, do not force a confrontation, and read the absence of a yes as a possible no
Multi-active — push harder emotionally to get a decision in the room
Linear-active — insist on the agenda and demand a logical justification
None of these — the behaviour is purely individual and carries no cultural information
questions.why: Not interrupting, avoiding confrontation and never losing face are the reactive markers. Pushing harder would risk exactly the embarrassment the reactive type avoids; the productive move is to give time and to read the indirect signals.

questions.q: Match each Hofstede dimension to what a high index means.
pairs: Striving for self-realization, belonging to the nuclear family, identification as "I"
Competition, success and performance as a driver
Effort to control the future and establish corresponding institutions
Fulfilment of desires and pleasures, one's own control over life and feelings
questions.why: Six dimensions, each scored 0–100, from studies in 93 countries. The low ends are the mirror image: "we" identity, work-life balance, acceptance that the future cannot be planned, flat hierarchies, tradition with demand for quick results, and restraint.

questions.q: A society accepts that the future cannot be planned and lives with uncertainty rather than building institutions against it. Which score does this describe?
options: Low uncertainty avoidance
High uncertainty avoidance
Low individualism
High power distance
questions.why: High uncertainty avoidance is the effort to control the future through institutions; accepting unplannability is the low end. This dimension is directly relevant in project work — it predicts how much detailed scheduling and contractual hedging a partner will expect.

questions.q: Match each pole to the cultural opposite the lecture pairs it with in the problem-solving process.
questions.why: Each pair is an axis on which teams silently differ. The pairs are not right-or-wrong: the practical point is that a mixed team must make its position on each axis explicit, otherwise every axis becomes a source of unexplained friction.

questions.q: Complete the figures on international (virtual) project teams.
questions.text: It takes over {{}} % longer to vote and make decisions, and {{}}–40 % more person-hours are needed for the communication effort.
questions.why: These numbers (Economist Intelligence Unit) turn culture from a soft topic into a schedule and cost item. They back the lecture's core claim: technical expertise alone is not enough in international projects.

questions.q: Which two obstacles does the lecture name as the biggest for successful collaboration?
options: Misunderstandings due to different cultural traditions, and various standards in the workplace
Insufficient technical training and outdated software
Currency risk and customs delays
Weak contract drafting and missing insurance
questions.why: The slide names cultural misunderstandings and differing workplace standards. The other options are real project risks but belong to Lectures 2, 4 and 6 — the point here is that the biggest obstacles are human, not technical.

questions.q: What is the term for the tendency to believe that one's own cultural views and methods are best and should be used as the standard?
questions.why: Ethnocentrism is the default failure mode of intercultural work — and the first three stages of Bennett's model (denial, defence, downplay) are all forms of it. The guest lecture adds the practical version: judging other cultures through the lens of one's own.

questions.q: Put Bennett's stages of intercultural competence development in order.
items: Denial — there is only one's own way
Defence — one's own way is the best way
Accept — there are different ways to do and see things
Adapt — use new methods to act more effectively
Integrate — smooth transition between different cultures
questions.why: The first three stages are ethnocentric, the last three ethnorelative; the move from downplay to accept is the decisive threshold. Note the trap in "downplay": claiming that differences do not matter still counts as ethnocentric, because it makes one's own standard the neutral default.

questions.q: A site manager says: "People are people everywhere — the cultural differences are really not that important, we all just want to build." Which Bennett stage is this?
options: Downplay — still ethnocentric
Accept — the first ethnorelative stage
Adapt
Integrate
questions.why: Minimising the differences is stage 3, the last ethnocentric one: the speaker's own frame is silently taken as the universal one. Acceptance would mean recognising that other ways of doing and seeing genuinely exist.

questions.q: How does the lecture frame conflicts in projects?
options: Conflicts are normal — what matters is how they are resolved
Conflicts must be prevented at all costs, since they always damage the project
Conflicts should be escalated to arbitration immediately
Conflicts only arise in teams without a clear hierarchy
questions.why: A successfully resolved conflict strengthens the group's consciousness and identity and develops the project positively; an escalated one produces dysfunctional cooperation, falling trust and mistrust. So the variable to manage is the resolution, not the occurrence.

questions.q: Which general requirements does the lecture set for personnel in international projects?
options: Great regional and mental flexibility
Language skills — very good to contract-proof
Tolerance towards other cultures and intercultural skills
Loyalty and the ability to balance conflicting interests
Head office knowledge and contacts
A doctorate in civil engineering
questions.why: Flexibility, contract-proof language, tolerance, loyalty, assertiveness, decision-making competence, contract reliability and head-office contacts make the list. Formal academic titles do not — the lecturer's own quote is "I did not graduate from any university, except the university of life".

questions.q: Sort each success factor into "posting design" (what the company controls) or "host country environment" (what it must live with).
items: Cultural distance from the home country
questions.why: The split is a management lesson: the left column is entirely in the company's hands, so failures there are self-inflicted. Note that the preparation should include the partner, and that return planning belongs to the posting design from the start.

questions.q: Put the phases of Tuckman's team-building model in order.
questions.why: Forming, storming, norming, performing, mourning. The lecture adds that the process starts anew — in a weakened form — whenever the team or the circumstances change, which in international projects happens constantly through rotation.

questions.q: Match each Tuckman phase to what characterises it.
pairs: Orientation, first acquaintance, courtesy, searching for one's own role — weak performance capability
Confrontation, task and role conflicts, power struggles or retreat (fight or flight) — but an important phase for moving forward
Search for solutions, open exchange and discussion, development of task assignments, processes and rules that fit the team; group cohesion
Full performance capability, constructive work style, identification as a team and mutual support
Project end, pride about the completed task, uncertainty about the future, farewell and dissolution of the group
questions.why: The counter-intuitive one is storming: the conflict phase is necessary, not a failure — the lecture calls it an important phase for moving forward. Performing is explicitly described as not achievable without going through the team-building process.

questions.q: Which actions can the project manager take in the intercultural team-building process?
options: Kick-off event
Information about the new culture
Organization of an intercultural training
Facilitating exchange
Allocation of tasks according to strengths
Driving the solution-finding process and setting common goals
Assigning each nationality to a separate work package to avoid friction
questions.why: The first four measures belong to the early phase (exchange of information, avoidance of stereotyping), the last two to the later phase (awareness of culture-specific strengths, commonly negotiated norms). Segregating nationalities is the opposite of the model, which aims at synergy effects and identification with the team.

questions.q: Order the three stages in the development of an intercultural project team.
items: Exchange of information and avoidance of stereotyping
Awareness of culture-specific strengths and commonly negotiated norms (language, …)
Use of synergy effects, identification with the team and innovative problem solving
questions.why: You cannot jump to synergy. First the team must exchange information and drop stereotypes, then negotiate its own norms — including which language it works in — and only then do the differences start paying off as innovative problem solving.

questions.q: Match each project area to the cultural question the lecture attaches to it.
pairs: In what form and how often are results recorded in writing?
What importance is placed on troubleshooting — is the culture action-oriented or results-oriented?
How high is the need for uncertainty avoidance?
How important is the informal information flow, and what is the project manager's role in the hierarchy?
How detailed is the scheduling, and how strictly is the plan adhered to?
Is the culture relationship-oriented — how much time is invested in building and maintaining good relationships?
questions.why: These six questions are the operational translation of Hofstede: uncertainty avoidance shows up in risk management, power distance in information management, relationship orientation in contact maintenance. Asking them at kick-off prevents the friction later.

questions.q: Which success factors for intercultural cooperation does the lecture list?
options: Good project organisation — clear tasks, responsibilities and processes
Willingness to accept constructive criticism
Positive basic attitude
Cultural awareness
Solid language skills
Identical professional background of all team members
questions.why: Five factors, and the summarising line is that all team members need a mixture of hard and soft skills. Uniform backgrounds are not a success factor — the whole point of the intercultural team is the synergy from diversity.

questions.q: Match each communication medium to what it is especially suitable for.
pairs: Information exchange and routine communications — fast and documentable, but risk of overload and no direct feedback
Information and formal agreements — formal and easy to document, but slow
Goal setting and team development — immediate direct feedback, at the price of coordination and travel expenses
Conflict management and issues of conflict — direct feedback and familiarity possible
Coordination and process planning — informal with direct feedback, but reduced communication channels
Exchange of views and brainstorming — economic and task-oriented, but with overlapping contributions
questions.why: The rule of thumb: the higher the conflict potential, the richer the medium must be. Conflict belongs face to face (or at least on video), routine belongs in email, and brainstorming tolerates the overlapping contributions of a chat.

questions.q: The lecture splits leadership into task-based and employee-related management. Which statement does it make about virtual teams?
options: The importance of employee-related leadership tasks increases in virtual teams
Task-based management fully replaces employee-related management
Leadership tasks can never be distributed within the team
Virtual teams need no leadership at all if the tools are good
questions.why: Distance removes the informal contact that normally sustains the social system, so the employee-related side has to be worked at deliberately. The lecture also notes that individual management tasks can be distributed within the team.

questions.q: Match each GLOBE leadership style to its markers.
pairs: Vision, motivation, inspiration, self-sacrifice, decisiveness, success orientation
Orientation towards the success of the entire team, integration of members, diplomatic and administratively competent, common understanding and goals
Involvement of team members in the preparation and implementation of decisions; delegation of tasks
questions.why: GLOBE (Global Leadership and Organizational Behavior Effectiveness) identifies six styles whose acceptance varies sharply by culture group. The conclusion the lecture draws: project managers in international projects must adapt their leadership behaviour accordingly.

questions.q: What does the acronym GLOBE stand for?
accept: global leadership and organizational behavior effectiveness
global leadership and organisational behaviour effectiveness
global leadership and organizational behaviour effectiveness
global leadership and organisational behavior effectiveness
questions.why: The study's name explains its logic: it measures which leadership behaviours are considered effective in which cultural region, rather than prescribing one universal ideal.

questions.q: Recall the lecturer's "some very subjective hints" for working abroad.
questions.answer:
• Be open-minded
  • Immerse yourself in other cultures
  • Meet other people at eye level
  • Be friendly and respectful
  • Humor creates connection and opens doors
  • Meet interesting people and build contacts with locals
  • Collect diverse impressions
  • Enjoy the cultural differences — especially the food
questions.why: These hints reappear verbatim in the Lecture 7 recapitulation, which makes them fair game for the exam despite their informal tone.

questions.q: Match each country to the "don't" the etiquette table gives for it.
pairs: Don't be overly personal or joke too much in business
Don't interrupt; don't write on someone's business card
Don't criticize openly; avoid political discussions
Don't rush into the agenda; don't expect punctuality
Don't use your left hand to give or receive; don't refuse hospitality
Don't offer a handshake to a woman unless she extends her hand first
questions.why: The table is a practical illustration of the Lewis and Hofstede axes: punctuality and directness (Germany, linear-active), face and hierarchy (Japan, China, reactive), relationship before agenda (Brazil, multi-active).

questions.q: The Midstad guest lecture argues for mixed-use development. What does the Berlin transaction data on the fragmentation index show?
options: The higher the fragmentation index, the higher the purchase price — a 0.1-point rise increases the price by about 3.47 %
Mixed use lowers the purchase price because it complicates management
The index has no measurable effect on price
Only office buildings benefit from a high index
questions.why: An index of 1.0 means maximum balance and diversity of uses within the building. The lecture's commercial argument is that a diverse range of uses raises both the selling price and the resilience of the asset — mixed use as a value driver, not just a planning ideal.

questions.q: What does the guest lecture mean by the "S" in ESG when it comes to urban redevelopment?
options: Social factors — schools, health centres and multi-purpose spaces enhance quality of life and acceptance
Sustainability certificates for the building envelope
Structural safety of the existing substance
Speed of the approval procedure
questions.why: The social component is presented as a hard value driver: acceptance and quality of life produce long-term added value and sustainable value stability for stakeholders — which is why urban concept advisory works at the interface of politics, business and society.

questions.q: Recall the "You should know" list for Culture and Leadership (as restated in Lecture 7).
questions.answer:
• Which intercultural competencies are necessary in international projects
  • What is culture? (iceberg model, culture types)
  • Leadership styles — what suits you and the team the most
  • Team management and communication ways
questions.why: The Lecture 7 recapitulation adds the explicit "What is culture? (iceberg model, culture types)" line to the original Lecture 3 list, so the iceberg and Lewis types are confirmed exam scope.

questions.q: What does FIDIC stand for in English?
accept: the international federation of consulting engineers
questions.why: FIDIC is an association of consulting engineers, not of contractors or clients — which is why its forms are drafted by independent consulting engineers and aim at a fair allocation of risk between the parties.

questions.q: Complete the FIDIC facts.
questions.text: FIDIC was founded in {{}} in Ghent by Belgium, France and Switzerland, has its headquarters in Geneva and produced its first standard form in {{}}. Its first edition of the Rainbow Suite of General Conditions appeared in {{}}, the second edition in {{}} — the earlier editions remaining valid.
questions.why: The dates matter in practice: because the 1999 editions remain valid alongside the 2017 ones, you must always check which edition a contract incorporates before relying on a clause number.

questions.q: Why do international projects use standard forms such as FIDIC instead of local contracts?
options: Consistency across borders — a well-established framework the parties can agree on
Balanced risk allocation that is perceived as neutral, building trust between parties
Neutral governing law and dispute resolution, e.g. arbitration in a third country
Investor and lender confidence — the World Bank and development banks use FIDIC as a standard form
Dispute resolution mechanisms such as early warnings and risk registers
Because FIDIC overrides the mandatory law of the host country
questions.why: Five good reasons plus modularity. But FIDIC never overrides mandatory law — the guest lecture is emphatic that mandatory law, permits, safety rules and public policy can override the contract.

questions.q: Which of these are listed as common misunderstandings about FIDIC?
options: "FIDIC is a law" — in fact the books are standard forms operating under a legal system, neither a legal system nor laws themselves
"FIDIC is the same as the VOB, just in English" — in fact FIDIC is not embedded in a specific legal jurisdiction
"The FIDIC books are the whole contract" — in fact they are only the General Conditions
"FIDIC contracts bind the parties" — in fact they are merely a non-binding recommendation
questions.why: The first three are the misunderstandings; the fourth is true, not a misunderstanding. FIDIC contracts do bind the parties — but legal provisions may change the interpretation given to the contract's provisions.

questions.q: A clause in the Particular Conditions conflicts with a mandatory safety regulation of the host country. What applies?
options: The mandatory law — it can override the contract, which is why you must ask both "what does the contract say?" and "what does the governing law require?"
The contract, because the parties freely agreed on it
Whichever the Engineer determines to be more economical
FIDIC's Golden Principles, which rank above national law
questions.why: The parties choose rules for cooperation and risk sharing, but mandatory law, permits, safety rules and public policy sit above that choice. The lecture's related point: FIDIC cannot conclusively regulate statutes of limitation or public law such as site safety, occupational health, environmental protection, customs and foreign exchange rules.

questions.q: Under FIDIC, which law governs the contract?
options: The law of the country specified in the Special / Particular Conditions
Always the law of the contractor's home country
Always Swiss law, because FIDIC is headquartered in Geneva
Always the law of the country where the works are executed
questions.why: The governing law is a choice the parties record in the Particular Conditions — which is why it is essential to specify it. In English law, moreover, a contract is a "legally binding agreement" that has the force of law between the parties and must be strictly observed.

questions.q: Match each FIDIC book to what it is for.
pairs: Construction contract — building and engineering works designed by the employer
Plant and Design-Build — works designed by the contractor
EPC / Turnkey projects with minimal employer input after award
Short form of contract for small-scale or simple works
Design, Build and Operate projects, with long-term operation by the contractor
The Red Book harmonised for projects funded by Multilateral Development Banks
Collaborative / alliance contracting, e.g. for underground works
questions.why: The colours encode who designs and how much the contractor takes on. Red = employer designs; Yellow = contractor designs; Silver = contractor designs and carries nearly everything; Gold adds operation; Green shrinks the whole thing; Pink, Blue and Emerald are specialised variants.

questions.q: Who carries the design responsibility in each book?
questions.why: The dividing line runs between Pink and Yellow. Green, Red and Pink are employer-design books (Pink is simply the MDB version of Red); from Yellow onwards the contractor designs — increasingly so, until under Gold it also operates what it designed.

questions.q: In which books does the contractor carry the responsibility for unforeseeable site conditions and for errors in the Employer's Documents?
options: Silver Book and Gold Book
Yellow Book and Silver Book
Red Book and Yellow Book
All books from Green onwards
questions.why: Design responsibility moves to the contractor already in the Yellow Book, but responsibility for errors in the Employer's Documents and for unforeseeable site conditions only moves across at the Silver Book. That step is exactly why the Silver Book is the expensive one for the employer — the contractor prices the geological risk it now owns.

questions.q: Order the books by increasing contractor's risk, and note what is added at each step.
items: Red Book — measured works, the baseline
Yellow Book — adds quantity risk and design risk
Silver Book — adds the risk for the tender documents and the full geological risk
Gold Book — adds the operating risk
questions.why: Each rung transfers one more class of uncertainty to the contractor, and each is priced. The commercial trade-off the Silver Book slide states plainly: the contractor takes the majority of risks and the employer pays more to cover them, in exchange for greater certainty on final price and completion date.

questions.q: An employer has completed the detailed design, provides a Bill of Quantities and wants to pay for measured quantities under the supervision of an Engineer. Which FIDIC book fits?
options: Red Book
Yellow Book
Silver Book
Gold Book
questions.why: Complete design plus BoQ plus payment by measurement against the rates and prices in the BoQ is the Red Book. The Yellow Book would price a lump sum against performance requirements, and the Silver Book has no BoQ at all.

questions.q: A lender-financed project must have maximum certainty on final price and completion date, with minimal employer involvement after award and a fully equipped facility ready to operate "at the turn of a key". Which book?
options: Silver Book
Red Book
Green Book
Blue Book
questions.why: "At the turn of a key" is the Silver Book's own wording for EPC/turnkey. The contractor performs all engineering, procurement and construction; administration is by the employer unless it appoints a representative; there is no Engineer.

questions.q: The employer wants a facility that the contractor designs, builds and then operates and maintains for about twenty years, awarded on whole-life cost and service levels. Which book?
options: Gold Book
Silver Book
Yellow Book
Pink Book
questions.why: Design, Build and Operate with long-term performance and maintenance (typically 20 years) is the Gold Book. Its award criteria — whole-life cost, performance guarantees, availability/service levels and the operational model — follow from the operating risk it transfers.

questions.q: A small, repetitive job of short duration and low capital value needs a contract without specialist sub-contracts and without an "Engineer". Which book?
options: Green Book — short form of contract
Red Book
Blue Book
Emerald Book
questions.why: The Green Book is for engineering and building work of relatively small capital value (suitable for works under about $500,000 or of limited duration). It makes no reference to "the Engineer" — the employer must nominate a spokesman or appoint a representative — and provides no advance payment.

questions.q: A World Bank–funded road project needs a construction contract with anti-corruption provisions, social safeguards and dispute boards built in. Which book?
options: Pink Book — MDB Harmonised Edition of the Red Book
Red Book, 1999 edition
Silver Book
Green Book
questions.why: The Pink Book is the Red Book harmonised with Multilateral Development Bank requirements — same underlying structure, plus the additional provisions the banks insist on. That is also why the guest lecture cites lender confidence as a reason for using FIDIC at all.

questions.q: Which features does the lecture give for the Blue Book (dredging and reclamation works)?
options: Applicable to any size and complexity of dredging and reclamation work
The works are designed by the employer or its Engineer, but contractor-designed works can also be included
A 'fitness for purpose' obligation
No remedying of dredging defects after completion
Dispute resolution by a Dispute Adjudication Board and ICC arbitration
No provision for advance payment
questions.why: The Blue Book does provide for advance payment — it is the Green Book that has none. The distinctive dredging features are the fitness-for-purpose obligation, the release of the dredging retention in full on completion, and the absence of defect remedying after completion (you cannot go back and fix a seabed).

questions.q: How does a Red Book contract come into effect?
options: When the Employer accepts the Tender by issuing the Letter of Acceptance; the parties may then sign a Contract Agreement
Only when both parties sign the Contract Agreement
When the Engineer issues the first payment certificate
On the Commencement Date fixed in the programme
questions.why: Red and Yellow Books come into effect with the Letter of Acceptance, with the Contract Agreement following as a formality. The Silver Book is the contrast: it comes into effect typically on signing the Contract Agreement, because there is no Engineer-administered tender acceptance in the same sense.

questions.q: Match each book to how payment is determined.
pairs: Interim and final payments determined by measurement, applying the rates and prices in the Bill of Quantities
Interim payments as specified in the Schedules of Payments; final payment based on the lump sum contract price
Lump sum contract price, with interim and final payments as work proceeds, usually against a Schedule of Payments
