No advance payment; interim payments in accordance with the value of works executed, with the retention percentage stated in the Appendix
questions.why: Measurement versus lump sum is the commercial spine of the suite. Under measurement the contractor is paid for what it actually did; under a lump sum it is paid for an agreed outcome — which is why the lump sum books also transfer quantity risk.

questions.q: Which books involve an Engineer, and which run with Employer and Contractor only?
questions.why: The Engineer exists where the employer needs someone to administer, certify and determine on its behalf — Red, Pink and Yellow. Green is too small to justify one, and Silver and Gold deliberately keep the employer out of the delivery so the contractor can own the outcome.

questions.q: Which statements about the Engineer are correct?
options: The Engineer is determined by the Employer — sometimes the Contractor does not even know who it is when entering into the Contract
The Engineer has the obligation to act fairly when making determinations or certifying payments
The Engineer is paid by the Employer and is therefore not completely impartial in reality
There is no direct contractual relationship between the Engineer and the Contractor
The Engineer is a party to the construction contract alongside Employer and Contractor
questions.why: The Engineer administers the contract on the Employer's behalf under a separate professional appointment — it is not a party to the construction contract and has no contractual link to the Contractor. The tension the guest lecture highlights is that it must act fairly while being paid by one side.

questions.q: Which are main tasks of the Engineer?
options: Certify — e.g. monthly invoices
Inspect — e.g. quality of the works
Review and approve — e.g. design, drawings, programme, Contractor's proposals
Instruct and determine — e.g. variations, suspensions, claims and extensions of time
Issue Taking-Over Certificates
Amend the Contract where it proves impractical
questions.why: Certify, inspect, give opinion, review, approve, valuate, instruct, determine and issue certificates. The one thing the Engineer explicitly cannot do is amend the Contract — nor relieve either party of any duty, obligation or responsibility under it.

questions.q: For which actions does the Engineer need the specific approval of the Employer?
options: Agreeing an Extension of Time and/or additional Cost
Instructing a Variation — except in emergencies and where it increases the Accepted Contract Amount by less than 1 %
Approving a proposal for a Variation by the Contractor
Specifying the amount payable in each of the applicable currencies
Inspecting the quality of the works on site
questions.why: The four approval-bound acts are the ones that cost the Employer time or money. Routine inspection needs no approval. Note the two carve-outs on variations: emergencies, and anything below the 1 % threshold of the Accepted Contract Amount.

questions.q: How must the Engineer proceed when making a Determination under sub-clause 3.7?
options: Consult with each Party in an endeavour to reach agreement; only if no agreement is achieved, make a fair determination in accordance with the Contract, taking due regard of all relevant circumstances
Decide immediately and without consultation, to save time
Refer the matter directly to the Dispute Board
Adopt the Employer's position, since the Employer pays its fee
questions.why: Consultation first, determination second — agreement is the preferred outcome and the determination is the fallback. This two-step is what makes the Engineer's decision reviewable and is the first rung of the escalation ladder.

questions.q: Under sub-clause 3.5 (Instructions of the Engineer), from whom shall the Contractor take instructions?
options: Only from the Engineer, or from a person to whom the appropriate authority has been delegated
From anyone on the Employer's side who is present on site
From the Engineer's Resident Engineer only
From the financier, where the project is externally funded
questions.why: Instructions must come through the contractually authorised route, and delegation must be proper. If an instruction constitutes a Variation, Clause 13 applies — which is why acting on an informal site instruction is a classic way to lose an entitlement.

questions.q: Put the documents forming a FIDIC contract into their typical order of precedence.
items: Particular Conditions Part A — Contract Data
Particular Conditions Part B — Special Provisions
questions.why: Precedence decides which document wins in a contradiction. Note the crucial consequence: the Particular Conditions rank above the General Conditions, so Part B can silently rewrite the FIDIC book you think you are working under.

questions.q: Match each contract document to what it does.
pairs: Short document naming the parties, formally concluding the Contract and listing the contract documents and sometimes the order of precedence
Simple document stating the sum of the offer and that it is binding until a stated date
Particular Conditions Part A — Contract Data
Mostly tabulated facts: time for completion, delay damages rate and cap, defects notification period, choice of law and language, dispute resolution mechanisms
Particular Conditions Part B — Special Provisions
All additions, deletions and changes to the General Conditions — may alter the contract significantly
Schedules of payments, execution programme, schedules of guarantees, possibly the BoQ
questions.why: Part A is where you look up the project's key numbers; Part B is where the danger lives. The lecture's worked example: replacing "42" with "20" in one paragraph lets the Employer unilaterally replace the Engineer — at worst nominating itself and undermining the entire intent of the contract.

questions.q: Why does the guest lecture single out Particular Conditions Part B as the document to read most carefully?
options: Because it contains all additions, deletions and changes to the General Conditions and may alter the initial contract significantly
Because it is the only document signed by both parties
Because it is drafted by FIDIC itself and cannot be negotiated
Because it sets the contract price
questions.why: Part B is where the standard form gets edited. The worked example shows an amendment on the replacement of the Engineer that hands the Employer unilateral power — the sort of change that looks like a formality and destroys the balance of the model.

questions.q: Which are the five FIDIC Golden Principles, introduced in 2019?
options: Keep duties, rights, roles and responsibilities consistent with the chosen book
Draft the Particular Conditions clearly and unambiguously
Do not change the risk allocation so far that the form becomes misleading
Preserve reasonable time periods for notices and procedures
Keep dispute avoidance and resolution mechanisms workable
Always choose the law of a European country as governing law
questions.why: Choice of governing law is free and is recorded in the Particular Conditions — it is not a Golden Principle. FIDIC introduced the principles in 2019 because of widespread misuse of its brand: heavily amended documents were still being called "FIDIC".

questions.q: What is the purpose of the Golden Principles, as the guest lecture frames it?
options: To preserve the logic of the standard form — Particular Conditions may tailor the deal, but excessive changes undermine the model
To make the FIDIC books legally binding without incorporation into a contract
To replace the General Conditions in projects above a certain value
To standardise the fees of consulting engineers
questions.why: The forms are built around an intended allocation of roles, risks and procedures. The principles are a warning against changing clauses without understanding the system — "do not judge a book by its cover" is the slide's own summary.

questions.q: The FIDIC sample contract framework is divided into three parts. Which?
options: General contract conditions; instructions for agreeing the special contract conditions; forms for tenders, the contract document and the dispute settlement agreement
Technical specification; bill of quantities; drawings
Employer's obligations; contractor's obligations; engineer's obligations
Pre-contract; execution; defects liability
questions.why: General conditions, guidance for drafting the particular conditions, and the forms. The middle part is what makes the suite adaptable without rewriting it from scratch — and what the Golden Principles then discipline.

questions.q: Match each General Conditions clause number to its subject in the 2017 edition.
pairs: Care of the Works and Indemnities
questions.why: The 2017 edition splits the old Clause 20 ("Claims, Disputes and Arbitration") into Clause 20 for claims and Clause 21 for disputes, and renames Force Majeure to "Exceptional Events" in Clause 18. In the 1999 Yellow Book, by contrast, Clause 19 was Force Majeure and Clause 20 covered claims, disputes and arbitration together.

questions.q: Sort the clauses into the thematic groups the guest lecture uses.
questions.why: Grouping the clauses is how the guest lecture recommends reading FIDIC: as a project-management system (who acts, when, for what money, and how it ends) rather than as a list of clause numbers to memorise.

questions.q: The contract states durations in days. Under sub-clause 1.1.3.9, what does "day" mean?
options: A calendar day — and a year means 365 days
A working day, excluding weekends and public holidays
Whatever the local labour law defines
A shift of eight working hours
questions.why: Defined terms exist precisely so that everyday assumptions do not creep in. The PM habit the lecture recommends: read the definitions before arguing about obligations, and quote the defined term exactly in notices and records.

questions.q: You receive an email and are unsure whether it counts as a valid contractual communication. What decides?
options: Whether the agreed system of electronic transmission is stated in the Appendix to Tender — communications must be in writing and delivered by hand against receipt, by mail or courier, or via an agreed electronic system
Whether the sender is a senior manager
Whether the email has a read receipt
Nothing — email is never a valid contractual communication
questions.why: The channel is contractually defined, so the answer is always "it depends on the Appendix to Tender". The related trap is treating an informal letter, email or site chat as a formal notice; the useful habit is setting up the communication matrix before work starts and keeping a decision log.

questions.q: Match each book to what the Employer tells the Contractor, per the guest lecture.
pairs: "Build exactly this" — complete design and drawings, materials and standards, construction methodology and a BoQ (RIBA stage 4, detailed design)
"Make it work like this" — performance requirements, key constraints and criteria, concept drawings and technical specifications (RIBA stages 2–3)
"Here is the outcome we want" — Employer's Requirements and output/functional specification, key performance criteria, no BoQ (RIBA stages 1–2)
"Here is the purpose and the service level" — functional objectives, performance outcomes and service levels, operational requirements, no BoQ (RIBA stages 0–1)
questions.why: The later the book's RIBA stage of employer input, the more design freedom — and risk — the contractor holds. Award criteria shift accordingly: Red on unit price, Yellow adding a technical proposal, Silver adding risk allowances and programme certainty, Gold on whole-life cost and service levels.

questions.q: Which sub-clause gives the overview of causes that may lead to an Extension of Time for Completion, and what is the catch?
options: Sub-clause 8.4 gives the overview, but the specific details for the different causes are found in different clauses
Sub-clause 8.4 is exhaustive and self-contained
Sub-clause 20.1 is the only source of extension entitlements
Extensions of time are always granted by the Dispute Board
questions.why: 8.4 is a signpost, not the whole map — variations, exceptional weather, unforeseen shortages and delays by the Employer are each detailed elsewhere. Note also that entitlements shrink as you move from Red to Yellow to Silver to Gold: the contractor has progressively fewer grounds for an extension.

questions.q: Put the variation process in order.
items: Trigger — the need for change appears
Instruction / proposal — authority and scope are clarified
Assessment — time, cost and risk impacts are evaluated
Record — the decision is documented and implemented
questions.why: The contract's job here is to separate authorised change from unmanaged drift. The process creates a record of what changed, why, who instructed it and how it affects price and programme — which is what makes the change defensible later.

questions.q: Which statement best captures the guest lecture's point about variations?
options: A change needs a time, cost and risk assessment — not just a technical instruction
Any change instructed on site is automatically a variation
Variations may only ever add work, never omit it
Variations do not require documentation if both parties agree verbally
questions.why: Quantities, quality, sequence, timing, omissions and additions may all change, but only the contractually authorised route should change the works, and the consequence must be assessed in all three dimensions. Verbal agreement leaves no record — the opposite of what the clause is for.

questions.q: What is the key idea behind the "change of law" provisions?
options: Fairness against the tender baseline — the parties priced the project under one legal environment, and the contract may adjust if that environment changes
The contractor must absorb all legal changes as part of its business risk
Any change of law automatically terminates the contract
Only changes in tax law are relevant
questions.why: Three questions follow from that idea: what law and conditions were assumed at tender (baseline), what cost/time/method change the new requirement caused (impact), and can the team show the link (record). Without the record the entitlement fails, however fair it may be in principle.

questions.q: Sort these into the measurement model or the lump sum model.
items: Pay for measured quantities; focus on quantities, rates and valuation
The governing question is "how much work was actually done?"
The Contract Price is the final price and follows the actual measured work
Pay for the agreed outcome; focus on scope definition and change control
The governing question is "is this within the agreed scope?"
The Contractor carries the quantity risk if the scope remains unchanged
questions.why: The pricing method changes incentives and the shape of disputes: under measurement you argue about quantities, under a lump sum about scope. The PM consequence is that the payment model and the change control must be designed together.

questions.q: Complete the definitions of the two price figures.
questions.text: The {{}} Contract Amount is the tender price. The Contract {{}} is the final price and follows the actual measured work — so under a lump sum with unchanged scope, the two are identical.
questions.why: Confusing the two is a classic error in claim correspondence. The Accepted Contract Amount is fixed at award and is also the reference for the Engineer's 1 % variation threshold; the Contract Price is what is actually payable at the end.

questions.q: Put the claims and disputes escalation ladder in order.
items: Notice of claim — preserve the right and alert the other party
Fully detailed claim — show entitlement, cause, impact and amount
Engineer's determination if no agreement is reached
Notice of dissatisfaction with the determination
Reference of the dispute to the DAAB and the DAAB's decision
questions.why: The lecture's advice is to remember the ladder rather than the day counts: notify, substantiate, consult, determine, dispute board, settlement, arbitration. Each rung must be climbed in turn — you cannot jump straight to arbitration.

questions.q: Match each step to its time limit in the 2017 sequence of events.
pairs: Within 28 days after becoming aware of the event
Within 84 days after becoming aware of the event
Within 42 days of submittal of the fully detailed claim
Notice of Dissatisfaction with the Determination (3.7.5)
Within 28 days after the Notice of Determination
Reference of Dispute to the DAAB (21.4.1)
Within 42 days after the Engineer's Determination
Notice of Dissatisfaction with the DAAB's decision (21.4.4)
Within 28 days after the DAAB's decision
questions.why: The pattern is easier than the list: 28 days to react to something, 42 days for an institutional step, 84 days to produce something substantial. Arbitration may only be started 28 days after the attempt at amicable settlement.

questions.q: What does "use it or lose it" mean for FIDIC claims?
options: A notice is mandatory, not optional — if it is not given in the required form and time, the party loses its entitlement (time bar)
A claim may be raised at any time until the final account is closed
Entitlement survives as long as the cost can be proved, regardless of timing
Only the Employer is subject to time bars
questions.why: Three rules: act early (notices are mandatory), act continuously (claims are managed throughout the project), act within time (late equals no entitlement). The rugby analogy on the slide: possession is only useful while the clock and the rules still allow the play.

questions.q: A claim is described as resting on three things. Which?
options: Entitlement, notice and substantiation
Delay, disruption and acceleration
Scope, schedule and budget
Notice, negotiation and litigation
questions.why: Entitlement asks which contract event gives time or money relief; notice asks whether the other party was informed in the required form and time; substantiation asks whether cause, effect and amount can be shown with records. All three must hold — a well-founded claim notified late is worth nothing.

questions.src: Lecture 4 · Guest lecture · The hidden half
questions.q: Which statements match the guest lecture's "hidden half of project management"?
options: Contracts do not solve problems — people do; a perfect contract does not prevent a poorly managed project
Most problems are behavioural, not technical, and issues escalate when communication breaks down
Complexity comes from stakeholders; alignment can be much harder than understanding the contract
Effective problem-solving is proactive — the best claims are the ones that never arise
As a PM you manage the contract, not the people
questions.why: The lecture's framing is the reverse of the last option: "as a PM you are not managing a contract — you are managing people, expectations and risk through it". The PM is described as a translator who manages expectations, not just tasks.

questions.q: Recall the five-point PM behaviour checklist that closes the contract law guest lecture.
questions.answer:
1. Know roles — clarify who instructs, certifies, determines and decides disputes; use the contract route.
  2. Notify early — send notices promptly, to the right party, in the right form; protect against time bars.
  3. Keep records — capture dates, instructions, progress, resources, costs and correspondence as events unfold.
  4. Manage change — connect scope, programme, price and risk; treat variations, claims and payment as one system.
  5. Escalate properly — consult and determine first, then move to DAAB, settlement or arbitration with evidence.

Habit to remember: if it changes the work, record it; if it affects time or money, notify it; if it remains unresolved, escalate it.
questions.why: This checklist is the guest lecture's own summary of how contract clauses translate into daily project habits.

questions.q: FIDIC basically distinguishes between two types of risk. Which?
options: Risks of physical loss or damage, and risks of financial or time loss
Insurable and uninsurable risks
Employer's risks and third-party risks
Foreseeable and unforeseeable risks
questions.why: Both types are then allocated to the parties in the risk, insurance and exceptional-events clauses. The allocation rule is asymmetric: the Employer's risks are the ones specified in the contract, and the Contractor carries all other risks.

questions.q: FIDIC treats risk in a logical sequence. Put it in order.
questions.why: The chain explains why insurance comes last: you first identify the risk, decide who is responsible, derive who is liable, agree who indemnifies whom, and only then insure the residual exposure. Buying insurance without settling responsibility gets the order wrong.

questions.q: Sort the contract types into price-based and cost-based remuneration.
items: Lump sum contract with bill of quantities (Detail-Pauschalvertrag)
Lump sum contract with schedule of works (Global-Pauschalvertrag)
Cost plus fee contract (cost plus percentage / fixed fee / fluctuating fee)
questions.why: Price-based contracts fix the price in advance (per unit or as a lump sum), cost-based contracts reimburse the actual cost plus a fee. Target contracts are the hybrid: cost-based in mechanics, but with a guaranteed maximum price or performance target steering the outcome.

questions.q: Put the course of an internationally tendered project in order.
items: Letter of acceptance / letter of award / contract agreement
Completion date / taking over / handing over
questions.why: The sequence has three gates: prequalification filters bidders, the letter of acceptance creates the contract, and taking over starts the defects notification period. In Germany, prequalification corresponds to Aufforderung zum Teilnahmewettbewerb / Teilnahmeantrag.

questions.q: Match each standard contract form to its origin and typical use.
pairs: Germany — public and private construction projects, integrated with German procurement law
United Kingdom — collaborative construction projects, emphasising cooperation and proactive management
United Kingdom — traditional design-bid-build contracts, known for detailed risk definitions
United States — a modular system, strong in architect-led building projects
Austria — risk allocation tailored to Austrian law
Switzerland — a norm-based system integrated into the Swiss legal framework
China — a statutory framework, often used in Belt-and-Road projects with local modifications
questions.why: Only FIDIC is genuinely international; the rest are national systems with varying export reach. NEC is the one with growing international relevance (UK, Hong Kong, New Zealand, South Africa) because it emphasises cooperation and proactive management.

questions.q: Which standard form does the overview table rate as having "very high" international relevance?
options: FIDIC — the global standard, especially with international financing institutions
VOB/B — the German procurement and contract regulations
JCT — Joint Contracts Tribunal
ConsensusDocs
questions.why: FIDIC is the only form rated "very high", explicitly because of its use with IFIs such as the World Bank. VOB/B and JCT are rated moderate (DACH region and UK/Commonwealth respectively) and ConsensusDocs low, being mostly US-based.

questions.q: Which qualities does the lecture claim for FIDIC contracts?
options: Clear and understandable — necessary clauses, detailed definitions, consistent structure
Fair and equal — risk distributed to the party that can bear, control and manage it
Designed and set up by independent consulting engineers
Complete and adaptable — the scope meets normal needs and adapts easily to specific requirements
Acknowledged — convincing reputation, worldwide acceptance, tested and proven
Legally binding worldwide without incorporation
questions.why: The five qualities are clarity, fairness, third-party drafting, adaptability and recognition. The risk principle is worth memorising in its exact form: risk goes to the party that can bear it, can control it and can manage it — not simply to the weaker party.

questions.q: What is the FIDIC Contracts Guide?
options: An official explanatory handbook published by FIDIC — a commentary and interpretation tool, not a contract itself
A binding annex that forms part of every FIDIC contract
The set of Particular Conditions for MDB-financed projects
A register of accredited FIDIC arbitrators
questions.why: Published in 2001, the Guide explains how the Red, Yellow and Silver Books work in practice. It is explicitly not a contract — quoting it will not win an argument that the contract wording does not support.

questions.q: The lecture distinguishes FIDIC Conditions of Contract from FIDIC Agreements. What is the difference?
options: Conditions of Contract govern the relationship between client and contractor; Agreements govern the relationship between client and consultants or subconsultants
Conditions of Contract are binding, Agreements are recommendations
Conditions of Contract apply abroad, Agreements only domestically
Agreements are for public projects, Conditions of Contract for private ones
questions.why: Two different contractual relationships, two different document families. The Conditions of Contract comprise General Conditions (core legal terms), Particular Conditions (project-specific modifications) and forms.

questions.q: "Two nations separated by a common language." Match each British English expression to what it actually means.
pairs: I disagree — although an American speaker would read it as "I understand"
Not very interesting — where American English means genuinely interesting
We are in severe trouble — not merely a rough patch
questions.why: The guest lecture uses these to make a contractual point: if ordinary English between two native varieties can diverge this far, then defined terms, written notices and traceable records are not bureaucracy — they are the only reliable channel.

questions.q: Recall the "You should know" list of Lecture 4, and the five questions the guest lecture wants you to answer.
questions.answer:
You should know:

  • Contracts according to FIDIC (and others)
  • The different FIDIC books and when to use them

The guest lecture's five questions:

  1. Why international contracts? — a shared system for cross-border projects
  2. Who decides? — roles and authority of Employer, Contractor and Engineer
  3. Who owns risk? — the books allocate design, site, time, price and operation risk
  4. What if reality changes? — variations, delay, payment and claims handle uncertainty
  5. How should PMs behave? — ask early, document clearly, notify on time, keep decisions traceable
questions.why: The guest lecture's roadmap is the best structure for revising this topic: read FIDIC as a project-management system, not as a list of clauses.

questions.q: Sort the megatrends we will face by 2030 into the global level and the construction-sector level.
items: Urbanisation — global migration to urban areas
Climate change — business as usual is being questioned
Demographic change — secure, attractive jobs for generations
Digitalisation — process efficiency through digital solutions
Industrialisation — investment in modular construction approaches and associated logistics
Climate resilience — new concepts for clients
questions.why: Three global drivers, three sector answers, and they pair up: urbanisation is met with industrialisation, climate change with climate resilience, and the demographic squeeze with digitalisation. The framing comes from the STRABAG Sustainability Strategy 2030.

questions.q: Complete the McKinsey survey figures on innovation fields for German business leaders.
questions.text: Artificial intelligence is the most important innovation field for {{}} % of German business leaders, followed by robotics at {{}} % and decarbonization technologies at {{}} %.
questions.why: The ranking is AI, robotics, decarbonization — with AI twice as often named as robotics. The quoted caveat matters as much as the numbers: value creation occurs where technologies are actually applied in practice, so innovations must be scaled and commercialized, not merely researched.

questions.q: The lecture points out that around 1900 about 38 % of cars in the USA were electric and 40 % steam-powered, with only 22 % running on gasoline — and that the first 3D-concrete-printed building was made in 1939. What is the point of these examples?
options: It is not enough to have a brilliant idea — it must also be implemented and scaled
Electric cars and 3D printing are technological dead ends
Innovation in construction is always faster than in the car industry
Old technologies are usually superior to new ones
questions.why: Both technologies existed long before they mattered commercially. The lecture uses them against the assumption that novelty equals progress: an invention only becomes an innovation once it is implemented, scaled and commercialized.

questions.q: Complete the fact about the first 3D-printed building.
questions.text: In {{}}, William E. Urschel created the world's first 3D concrete printed building in Valparaiso, Indiana. His machine automated the mixing, pouring and {{}} of concrete.
questions.why: The Lecture 7 recapitulation returns to this slide with the line "3D printing has not just been invented!" — a reminder that the construction industry's innovation problem is adoption, not invention.

questions.q: AutoCAD is used as the counter-example of an innovation that did scale. Which reasons does the lecture give?
options: Released in 1982, it ran on ordinary PCs (MS-DOS) rather than on expensive workstations
In the 1980s it made CAD software affordable for smaller offices and engineers
By the 1990s it had become the industry standard (DWG standard)
The system is relatively inexpensive, modular, expandable and compatible
It was mandated by law for all public building projects
questions.why: Affordability, the ordinary hardware base, modularity and compatibility drove adoption — by 1994 there were 750 AutoCAD training centres. No legal mandate was involved, which is exactly why it is a persuasive example of market-driven scaling.

questions.q: Match each pillar of STRABAG's Strategy 2030 to its content.
pairs: We build for people and with people — each project creates added value for our colleagues and for society
Working to combat climate change, guided by the desire to make projects climate neutral by 2040 and to intensify construction in the energy sector
A technology pioneer in construction — thinking ahead, data-driven decision-making and questioning the status quo to develop new expertise
questions.why: The three pillars map onto the classic sustainability triad: social, environmental and technological/economic. Note that the climate-neutrality target of 2040 is anchored in the middle pillar, not treated as a side project.

questions.q: What characterises SID — STRABAG Innovation & Digitalisation?
options: A centralized division reporting directly to the CEO
Drives the digital transformation — BIM, 5D, GIS, robotics
Innovates within construction
Serves as internal consultant and enabler
Fosters digital culture and sustainability
Operates as an external consultancy selling services to competitors
questions.why: The reporting line to the CEO is the structural point: digitalisation is positioned as a governance matter, not a technical support function. SID acts internally as consultant and enabler rather than as an external service provider.

questions.q: At the Schils power plant in Switzerland (2019–2020), which four processes were carried out model-based?
options: Excavation, using 3D excavator control
Survey and setting-out
Formwork and reinforcement work
Digital acceptance
Payroll accounting for the site staff
questions.why: The pilot was the first paperless construction site using only 3D execution models: planned and executed collaboratively with the OpenBIM method, with reinforcement and formwork erected from an IFC model on a tablet. Payroll is not a model-based construction process.

questions.q: Which open data format was used on a tablet at the Schils site to install and erect reinforcement and formwork?
questions.why: IFC is the vendor-neutral exchange format behind the OpenBIM method — using it rather than a proprietary format is what made a genuinely collaborative, paperless site possible across all the parties involved.

questions.q: The lecture says construction projects are increasingly designed and built according to circular principles. What does it name as the decisive influence on whether circular-economy methods are actually applied?
options: It is project-dependent and significantly influenced by the clients' requirements
It depends solely on the contractor's internal sustainability targets
It is fully prescribed by EU regulation
It depends on the availability of recycled steel
questions.why: The demand side drives it — which is why an extract from a 2025 prequalification is shown as evidence. Clients are already asking for circularity and CO₂e information in tenders, so it becomes an award criterion rather than a voluntary extra.

questions.q: Match each label to the share of the construction and real-estate industry the lecture gives.
questions.why: Two fifties and two forties — materials and waste at ~50 %, energy and CO₂ at ~40 %. These four figures are the quantitative basis for the "special role of the construction industry" named in the Lesson Learned list, and for the closing claim that the industry is not only part of the problem but also part of the solution.

questions.q: Roughly what percentage of the world's waste is generated by the construction industry?
questions.why: Around 50 % — the same order of magnitude as its share of global material requirements. Lecture 1 adds the cradle-to-grave figure of 38 % of global carbon emissions for the construction industry specifically, against ~40 % for construction and real estate together.

questions.q: Why does the lecture put life cycle cost on the "You should know" list?
options: Because the initial construction cost is only a fraction of the cost a building causes over its life, so decisions must be judged over the whole cycle
Because life cycle cost is identical to the tender sum
Because operating cost is irrelevant once the building is handed over
Because it only applies to infrastructure, not to buildings
questions.why: First cost versus follow-up cost is the whole point of the slide: the follow-up costs dominate. This is also what makes the Gold Book (design, build and operate) and circular design economically rational rather than merely virtuous.

questions.q: How does the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change define climate neutrality, as quoted in the lecture?
options: Endeavour to minimize greenhouse gas emissions as much as possible and to offset unavoidable emissions through systematic offsetting measures
Emitting no greenhouse gases whatsoever at any point in the value chain
Buying enough carbon certificates to cover all emissions, without reducing them
Reducing emissions by at least 50 % against a 1990 baseline
questions.why: The definition has two halves in a fixed order: minimize first, offset only what remains unavoidable. Offsetting alone (option 3) is not climate neutrality, and the definition does not require literal zero emissions.

questions.q: Put STRABAG's climate-neutrality milestones in chronological order.
items: 2040 — climate-neutral building materials and infrastructure; climate neutrality along the entire value chain
questions.why: The sequence runs from what is easiest to control to what is hardest: own offices first, then a project, then operation, and only last the materials and the whole upstream value chain — where most of the emissions actually sit.

questions.q: Order the four levers on the path to CO₂e reduction, from avoidance to compensation.
items: Resource-efficient and long-lasting construction — CO₂-reduced buildings, circular buildings, building within existing buildings
Ecological and climate-friendly building — climate-neutral production, renewable raw materials, transformation of energy
Efficient construction and operation — digitization, efficient methods such as prefabrication and LEAN, renewable energies
Intelligent compensation — CO₂ certificates and carbon capture
questions.why: Avoidance of CO₂ comes first and compensation last — the same logic as the UNFCCC definition. Buying certificates is the residual step for what could not be avoided, not a substitute for the first three levers.

questions.q: Which of these are among the eight action areas for energy consumption in the construction industry?
options: Buildings — climate-neutral operation of administration buildings used by the group
Passenger cars and commercial vehicles — conversion of the fleet to renewable energy sources
Construction site power and other construction-related energy — electrification of small equipment, office containers and cranes
Construction machinery and heavy goods vehicles — conversion to renewable energy sources
Asphalt mixing plants, stone and gravel plants, concrete plants and other production — conversion to renewable energy sources
Efficiency increase through conversion to new technologies such as electrification
Relocation of production to countries with lower energy prices
questions.why: The eight areas cover buildings, vehicles, site power, machinery, the three plant types and efficiency. Relocating emissions abroad is not a reduction at all — it contradicts the commitment to climate neutrality along the entire value chain.

questions.q: What accompanies the greenhouse-gas reduction pathway to make it verifiable?
options: Key actions linked to targets for 2030 and 2040 defined for each action area
Definition of specific metrics to monitor implementation and effectiveness
Monitoring and reporting
An annual target/actual comparison of the metric
A one-off audit at the end of the pathway in 2040
questions.why: Targets per action area, metrics, monitoring and an annual target/actual comparison. A single audit at the end would make deviations undetectable until it is too late — the same early-warning logic that Lecture 6 applies to project risk.

questions.q: Which goals does the lecture set for a circular economy in construction?
options: Consider buildings over their entire life cycle — saving raw materials, increasing efficiency, using secondary or renewable raw materials, avoiding waste
Develop end-to-end material and waste concepts and introduce a waste management system that also covers hazardous waste
Continuously increase the percentage of recycled materials and investigate alternative, renewable building materials

During design and build, consider not only the origin of materials but also their possible uses at the end of their service life — materials and components should be removable, separable and reusable or recyclable
Extend the linear model of extraction, use and disposal to make it more efficient
questions.why: The whole premise is that the linear system of extraction, use and disposal is reaching its limits, so making it "more efficient" is not a circular goal. The design-stage requirement — removable, separable, reusable — is the one that determines whether circularity is possible at all decades later.

questions.q: Besides the environmental argument, which business opportunity does the lecture see in reuse and recycling of raw materials?
options: It reduces procurement and disposal costs and opens new business areas, e.g. sustainable building materials and refurbishment of existing buildings
It removes the need for a waste management system
It eliminates the need for structural design
It makes demolition unnecessary
questions.why: Circularity is presented as commercially self-interested, not merely regulatory: lower cost at both ends of the material flow, plus new revenue in sustainable materials and in building within existing buildings.

questions.q: Which framework of the circular economy — named after the number of strategies it contains, each beginning with the same letter — does the lecture present?
questions.why: The 9R framework orders the strategies from the most to the least valuable — refuse and rethink at the top, recycle and recover at the bottom. Recycling is therefore the weakest circular strategy, not the goal, which is why the lecture pairs it with material efficiency strategies across the product life cycle.

questions.q: Why is CO₂e estimation entering the tender process?
options: Strategic orientation towards sustainability — the company is striving for climate neutrality in 2040
Increasing customer requirements — public and private clients already demand CO₂e information
Lack of standards and tools in the construction industry, since different methodologies and emission factors are still used
Because CO₂e reporting replaces the bill of quantities
questions.why: Two pulls (own strategy, client demand) and one problem (no common methodology). The missing standard is what makes the CCF/PCF distinction and consistent life-cycle modules necessary — otherwise two bidders' CO₂e figures are not comparable.

questions.q: Sort each statement into corporate carbon footprint or product carbon footprint.
items: Sum of greenhouse gases emitted and removed in the course of business activities
Relates to the reporting period of a company
Captured and analysed at STRABAG using the in-house CarbonTracker software
Sum of greenhouse gases emitted and removed in a product system
Covers the entire life cycle of a product
Calculated by multiplying a quantity by an environmental impact indicator value per life-cycle module
questions.why: The dividing question is the unit of account: CCF measures a company over a reporting period, PCF measures a product over its life cycle. Both are expressed in CO₂e, which is why they are easy to confuse in a tender.

questions.q: For 100 m³ of concrete C30/37, match each life-cycle module to its contribution in kg CO₂e.
questions.why: Module D is negative — it credits the benefit of recovery beyond the system boundary, and is the only module that reduces the total. The sum is 27,894 kg CO₂e, of which the product stage A1–A3 alone accounts for over 90 %: the material choice, not the transport, dominates.

questions.q: In the 100 m³ C30/37 example the modules sum to 27,894 kg CO₂e. Which conclusion follows for a project manager?
options: The product stage A1–A3 dominates, so the biggest lever is the choice and specification of the material itself
Transport to site (A4) is the biggest lever, so local sourcing solves the problem
Module D outweighs the others, so recycling alone makes the concrete climate neutral
End-of-life (C1–C3) dominates, so demolition planning is the main lever
questions.why: A1–A3 contributes 25,930 of 27,894 kg CO₂e. A4 is 204 kg and module D credits only −399 kg, so neither transport nor recovery can compensate for a carbon-heavy specification — the decision that matters is made when the concrete is specified.

questions.q: Which example does the lecture use to argue that the construction industry is "not only part of the problem, but also part of the solution"?
options: Microtunneling for carbon capture storage projects — shore crossings for pipelines
Replacing concrete with timber in all structures
Closing asphalt mixing plants
Reducing the number of construction projects
questions.why: The decarbonisation infrastructure itself — CCS pipelines, pumped storage, grid connections — has to be built by someone. The Hatta pumped storage plant in Dubai is shown on the following slide as the second example of the same argument.

questions.q: Which key facts about dams and hydropower does the guest lecture give for the 2050 best case?
options: Carbon neutrality can only be guaranteed if the installed hydropower capacity doubles
There are approximately 9,000 dams worldwide, of which only about 25 % are used for electricity generation
Construction surged in the 1950s and peaked in the 1970s, so the timeframe available now is 25 years rather than 75
The best locations are already taken, so alternative locations imply severe hazards such as environmental impact and climate change
Sedimentation and the decommissioning of ageing dams are already fully accounted for in these figures
questions.why: The figures explicitly do not consider sedimentation or the decommissioning of ageing dams — so the real challenge is larger than doubling. The 25-versus-75-year point is the sharpest: the same expansion that historically took three quarters of a century must now happen in a quarter of one.

questions.q: Sort the properties of hydropower into advantages and disadvantages.
items: Renewable, with very low direct CO₂ emissions once constructed
Long lifespan of more than 100 years
questions.why: The economics are the mirror image of the environmental profile: very high CAPEX and very low OPEX over a 100-year life. That cost shape is exactly why hydropower needs long-tenor, often ECA- or development-bank-backed financing of the kind covered in Lecture 2.

questions.q: Match each turbine type to its flow characteristics.
pairs: Axial flow — low head (1–80 m) and high flow (up to 900 m³/s)
Mixed flow — medium-to-high head (15–700 m) and medium-to-high flow
Jet flow — high head (up to 1,000 m) and low flow
questions.why: Head and flow are inversely related across the three: Kaplan for a lot of water falling a little, Pelton for a little water falling a long way, Francis in between. Run-of-river schemes therefore use Kaplan or cross-flow turbines.

questions.q: Match each hydropower configuration to its description.
pairs: Only a weir is required; Kaplan or cross-flow turbines
The turbine is placed directly in the flowing water
Increases energy output by increasing the head, and provides storage — the key to continuous generation
questions.why: The progression is about storage. Run-of-river and in-stream systems take what the river gives at that moment; only a conventional dam creates the head and the reservoir that make generation controllable.

questions.q: Sort each example dam into its structural type.
questions.why: The concrete family has five sub-types (gravity, buttress, arch, double-arch and roller-compacted concrete); masonry, earthfill and rockfill are separate categories. The guest lecturer worked on both JIF07 in Oman and Thiba in Kenya.

questions.q: Sort the watertight elements of a fill dam by where they sit.
questions.why: Both positions can use asphalt, which is why the material alone does not identify the design — the position of the watertight element does. A geocomposite is only ever an upstream-face solution.

questions.q: Complete the facts on the Goldisthal pumped storage plant.
questions.text: Goldisthal in Germany, completed in {{}}, is the largest German pumped storage plant with {{}} MW and can deliver full power for up to {{}} hours. As a rule of thumb, 1 MW supplies {{}} to 1,000 homes.
questions.why: The 8-hour figure is the important one: pumped storage is not a battery for seconds but a store for a working day, which is what makes it the complement to solar and wind. At 750–1,000 homes per MW, Goldisthal covers roughly a million households while discharging.

questions.q: Which statements about pumped storage hydro (PSH) are correct?
options: A scheme can be open-loop or closed-loop, operating in pump mode or turbine mode
It is ideal in combination with solar and wind
Storage of renewable energy is key to the 2050 carbon-neutrality scenario
Coire Glas in Scotland is planned for 1,500 MW
It generates more energy than it consumes over a full pump-turbine cycle
questions.why: PSH is a store, not a source: pumping consumes more energy than turbining returns. Its value lies in shifting renewable generation in time — which is why Scotland has a pipeline of schemes (Earba 1,800 MW, Coire Glas 1,500 MW, Loch Kemp 600 MW, Loch na Cathrach 450 MW) starting in 2027/28.

questions.q: Why is the Kidston project in Australia presented as an approach to sustainability?
options: A former gold mine, closed in 2001, was reused for a 250 MW pumped storage scheme plus a 50 MW solar farm, commissioned in 2025
It was the first dam built entirely from recycled concrete
It replaced a coal-fired power station on the same site
It is the world's largest run-of-river scheme
questions.why: Reusing the pits of a mine discovered in 1907 and closed in 2001 avoids new excavation and new land take entirely — circular thinking applied at the scale of infrastructure, and a neat pairing of storage with the co-located solar farm.

questions.q: The guest lecture calls pumped storage a "proven technology" over 40 years old. Which examples support this?
options: Cruachan Power Station (440 MW, 1965) and Dinorwig "Electric Mountain" (1,700 MW, 1984)
Goldisthal (2003) and Kidston (2025)
Hatta, Dubai (2025) and Thiba, Kenya (2022)
Coire Glas and Earba, both planned for 2027/28
questions.why: Cruachan and Dinorwig have been running since 1965 and 1984 — the point being that nothing new has to be invented, only built. The other options are either recent, planned, or not pumped storage at all (Thiba is an irrigation dam).

questions.q: For the European power generation mix in 2022/23 the guest lecture gives >24 % fossil fuels and 24 % nuclear. What share does it give hydro?
options: 17 %, alongside 13 % solar and 17 % wind
40 %, the largest single source
5 %, a negligible contribution
24 %, equal to nuclear
questions.why: Hydro at 17 % already matches wind and exceeds solar — it is not a marginal source. That existing base is why doubling installed hydropower capacity is presented as achievable, if difficult, by 2050.

questions.q: Recall the "You should know" list of Lecture 5.
questions.answer:
• Main challenges and trends in the construction industry
  • The special role of the construction industry
  • Life cycle cost
  • Basics of the circular economy

"Special role" refers to the four shares: ~50 % of global material requirements, ~40 % of energy demand, ~40 % of CO₂ emissions and ~50 % of the world's waste — the industry is both a major cause and a necessary part of the solution.
questions.why: This is the stated exam scope for Lecture 5; the guest lecture on water, dams and pumped storage is explicitly exam-relevant on top of it.

questions.q: The lecture pairs four risk groups in traditional construction work abroad with four hedging instruments. Match them.
questions.why: Each instrument answers a different kind of exposure: you price what you can calculate, you allocate by contract what you can negotiate, you insure what is statistically tractable, and you secure with third-party guarantees what neither party can control.

questions.q: Sort each risk from the risk map into its category.
items: Fluctuating exchange rates and high inflation
Foreign exchange restrictions and supply embargos
Unpredictability of the market and funding
Short-term changes to laws and regulations
Different technical standards and technological requirements
Different understanding of project management and its tools
questions.why: Six categories — and all of them come in addition to the "usual" construction risks, which is precisely what makes international work harder. Note that technical and technological differences are classed as legal risks, because they enter the project through standards and regulations.

questions.q: ISO 31000 defines risk as the "effect of uncertainty on objectives". What is the notable consequence the lecture draws from this wording?
options: The deviation from the expected can be positive, negative or both — many other definitions consider only the negative deviation
Risk exists only where a loss has already occurred
Risk and uncertainty are synonyms
Only measurable financial effects count as risk
questions.why: The ISO definition is deliberately two-sided, which is why the practical tool is a Risk and Opportunities register with both a negative and a positive risk value column. Risk is usually expressed in terms of risk sources, potential events, consequences and likelihood.

questions.q: Match each ISO 31000 term to its definition.
pairs: Coordinated activities to direct and control an organization with regard to risk
Element which alone or in combination has the potential to give rise to risk
Occurrence or change of a particular set of circumstances
Outcome of an event affecting objectives
Measure that maintains and/or modifies risk
questions.why: The terms form a causal chain: a source can produce an event, whose consequence affects objectives, with a certain likelihood, and a control is what you insert into that chain. Writing a register in these terms is what makes risks comparable.

questions.q: Complete the working formula for risk.
questions.text: Risk = {{}} of an event × {{}} of occurrence of the event.
questions.why: Impact times probability is what turns a list of worries into a ranked, monetised register — and it is the same formula the Technical Controlling guest lecture uses as "probability (%) × amount (€) = risk exposure".

questions.q: In the risk register extract, a geology and hydrology risk (infiltration, injection and drainage due to leakages in a retaining wall) has an affected amount of €1,000,000, 100 % of it affected, and a probability of 50 %. What is the risk value?
questions.why: €1,000,000 × 100 % affected × 50 % probability = €500,000. The register separates the three factors deliberately: the gross amount at stake, the share of it actually exposed, and the likelihood — so that changing any one of them can be traced.

questions.q: Why are construction projects associated with particularly high risks?
options: High complexity and many stakeholders
Uniqueness of the project
Long project duration
External influences and high investment
Technical uncertainties
Legal and contractual risks
Because construction work is performed by a single trade
questions.why: Eight reasons: complexity, stakeholders, uniqueness, duration, external influences, high investment, technical uncertainty and legal/contractual risk. The opposite of the last option is true — the many interacting trades and interfaces are a source of risk, not a mitigation.

questions.q: Complete the Latham quote.
questions.text: "No construction project is risk free. Risk can be managed, minimised, shared, transferred or accepted. It cannot be {{}}."
questions.why: The quote is the lecture's mission statement: every listed verb is an active choice, and the only option not available is doing nothing. Ignoring a risk does not remove it — it merely removes your ability to price or control it.

questions.q: Stuttgart 21 was estimated at about €2.5 bn in the 1995 feasibility study with commissioning in 2008. What do the 2026 figures show?
options: €14.5 bn and commissioning in December 2031 — roughly +480 % on cost and +23 years on schedule
€6.5 bn and commissioning in 2022 — roughly +160 % and +14 years
€9.15 bn and commissioning in December 2025 — roughly +266 % and +17 years
Cost and schedule were both held within 20 % of the original estimate
questions.why: The two summary figures on the slide are +480 % on cost and +23 years on schedule. The intermediate values (€6.5 bn in 2013, €9.15 bn in 2022, €11.5 bn in 2025) are real waypoints in the escalation, but the headline comparison is 1995 against 2026.

questions.q: Which are among the main reasons the lecture gives for the Stuttgart 21 cost and schedule overruns?
options: Initial cost estimate too low
Tunnelling and geology
Design changes and technical enhancements
Increases in construction costs and inflation
Digitalization and control systems
Pandemic and supply chain impacts
Lawsuits and approval processes
Insolvency of the main contractor
questions.why: Seven causes are listed — contractor insolvency is not among them. Note the ordering: the very first cause is an estimate that was too low from the start — an error made before a single metre was excavated, which no amount of later site management could repair.

questions.q: With professional risk management these risks could have been avoided or mitigated. Which measures does the lecture name?
options: Realistic cost estimates free from political influence
Early and detailed assessment of geological risks
Provision for adequate risk reserves, cost contingencies and time buffers
Continuous risk monitoring throughout the project lifecycle
Transparent communication among all stakeholders
Awarding the contract to the lowest bidder in every package
questions.why: Five mitigations, and the first names the real cause: political influence on the estimate. Awarding purely on lowest price is the COVEC failure mode from Lecture 1 — it increases risk rather than mitigating it.

questions.q: The lecture divides risk potential into five groups. Sort each risk into its group.
items: Strategic risks, investment and participation policy
Corporate planning, organization, accounting and reporting
Faulty control systems and legal violations
Warranty and liability risks; freight and transport
Country risks, political and legislative risks
Currency risks, customs regulations, import and export restrictions
Natural catastrophes and comparable unforeseeable events
questions.why: The five groups separate risks by where they originate: management (own decisions), operations (own execution), external environment, force majeure, and the client relationship. That origin determines who in the organization can actually do something about them.

questions.q: Put the eight steps of the risk management process (after Hoffmann) in order.
items: Risk identification — risk categories and individual risks, by cause
Risk analysis — consequence, probability, level, measures
Risk treatment — avoid, reduce, shift, accept
questions.why: The ISO 31000 version of the same loop wraps communication & consultation and monitoring & review around the core sequence (scope/context/criteria → identification → analysis → evaluation → treatment → recording & reporting) rather than placing them at the end — they run continuously, not once.

questions.q: In the ISO 31000 diagram, what is the role of "communication & consultation" and "monitoring & review"?
options: They run alongside the entire process rather than being single steps at the end
They are the first and last steps respectively
They apply only at corporate level, not at project level
They replace risk documentation
questions.why: Both flank the whole risk-assessment sequence in the diagram. That layout carries the lecture's message: risk management is a continuous loop, and risks that were once assessed as harmless can suddenly become a threat to success.

questions.q: Sort each risk into company-level or project-level risk management.
questions.why: The same eight-step process runs at both levels, but on different objects. Some risks appear on both lists in different guises — health & safety compliance is a corporate risk, a health & safety incident is a project risk.

questions.q: How is risk management integrated into the organizational structure of a large construction company?
options: A staff position for risk management coordination at company management level, plus staff positions for risk management at each division
A single risk manager inside each project team, with no company-level function
It is outsourced entirely to the insurer
It is handled by the site managers alongside their other duties
questions.why: Large companies have a coordinating staff position at the top and one per division, above the project organisations. Medium-sized companies or individual divisions collapse this into a single staff position for risk management next to company or division management.

questions.q: The influenceability curve shows roughly 35 %, 38 % and 22 % of cost-influencing potential across the project. What is the management conclusion?
options: Risks must be identified as early as possible, because the ability to influence cost collapses as the project progresses while the investment cost accumulates
Cost can be influenced equally at any stage, so early planning is optional
The greatest influence lies in the construction supervision phase
Influenceability rises towards the end of the project
questions.why: The curve of cost potential influence falls steeply while the development of investment costs rises — the scissors that define construction economics. By the time you are on site, most of the money is already committed by decisions taken in the optimization phases.

questions.q: Put the nine HOAI work phases in order.
items: Participation in awarding contracts (Mitwirkung bei der Vergabe)
Project supervision and documentation (Objektbetreuung und Dokumentation)
questions.why: HOAI — the German fee structure for architects and engineers — defines these nine classic phases. They matter for risk because the influenceability curve is plotted against them: phases 1–3 are where cost is decided, phases 8–9 where it is merely recorded.

questions.q: Match each optimization phase to what it is about.
pairs: To assess solutions — optimization during planning
Turning ideas into reality — tendering, pre-qualification of executing companies, negotiations, contracts
questions.why: The three phases run in parallel with the falling influenceability curve. By phase 3 you are contracting, so the remaining lever is contractual allocation of risk rather than technical optimisation.

questions.q: In the risk map (risk classification), how are the axes defined and where does the acceptance boundary run?
options: Probability of occurrence against damage — risks in the low/low corner are acceptable, risks towards high/high are too high
Cost against schedule — anything above the diagonal is acceptable
Probability against controllability — only uncontrollable risks are plotted
Damage against insurance premium — everything insurable is acceptable
questions.why: The map plots probability of occurrence against extent of damage, with a diagonal band separating "risk acceptable" from "risk too high". Its value is that it makes a heterogeneous list comparable — and forces a decision on everything above the line.

questions.q: Sort each risk assessment method into its group.
items: Brainstorming — identification and analysis in the team
Damage analysis of past projects and risks
Indicator analysis — change indicators, e.g. dealing with changed market prices
Scenario analysis — description of alternative states, "learning from the future"
Standard deviation — interpretation of costing and pricing
Monte Carlo simulation — aggregation of individual risks to estimate the total risk
questions.why: The four groups differ in what knowledge they tap: explicit knowledge and a known risk horizon (empirical data), implicit knowledge and expert competence (creativity), past experience (retrospective) and distributions (statistics). A good process combines them — checklists alone can only find risks somebody has already met.

questions.q: According to the methods table, which methods are rated strongest for assessment (rather than identification)?
options: Standard deviation and Monte Carlo simulation
Checklist and list of damages
Damage analysis and retrospective analyses
Brainstorming alone
questions.why: The two statistical methods score highest on assessment and weakest on identification — they can quantify a risk but cannot find one. Checklists and damage lists are the mirror image: strong at identification, weak at assessment. That is exactly why the groups are complementary.

questions.q: Which simulation method is used to aggregate individual risks into an estimate of the total risk, using distribution functions for scenario planning?
questions.why: Individual risks cannot simply be added, because they interact and rarely all occur at once. A Monte Carlo simulation samples the distributions repeatedly to produce a realistic range for the total — which is what makes a defensible contingency figure possible.

questions.q: Order the four risk treatment strategies as the lecture numbers them, from the total risk down to what remains.
items: Shift — transfer of hazards, insurances, contractual clauses
questions.why: The order is a funnel: what you cannot avoid you reduce, what you cannot reduce you shift, and only the remainder is knowingly accepted. "Accepted hazards" are therefore a deliberate residue — which the Principles of risk-conscious action qualify further: we only accept controllable risks.

questions.q: Match each treatment strategy to its example from construction practice.
pairs: No offer in the case of a client with low creditworthiness
questions.why: Note where every path ends: whether you decrease, shift or accept, the residual lands "→ Calculation". Risk management in tendering is ultimately a pricing exercise — the only strategy that keeps a risk out of the price entirely is avoidance.

questions.q: The specification says: "Any necessary dewatering measures shall be provided by the Contractor without separate remuneration." The cover letter replies: "We have calculated open dewatering with a flow rate of up to 10 m³/h in our service. Any additional dewatering services required are to be paid for separately." Which strategy is this?
options: Decreasing — concretization in the cover letter
Avoiding — exclusion in the cover letter
Shifting — transfer to an insurer
Accepting — full inclusion in the price
questions.why: The bidder does not exclude dewatering, it quantifies it — capping the accepted exposure at 10 m³/h. Full avoidance would be the other wording on the slide: "we have not taken into account any dewatering measures … these would have to be paid for separately if required".

questions.q: Where do identified and unidentified risks appear in the bid build-up?
options: Identified risks are covered as an element of costing — in direct costs and site overheads; unidentified risks are covered as an element of pricing — in the venture and profit surcharge
Both are covered in the value added tax
Identified risks go into profit, unidentified risks into direct costs
Neither is included; risks are handled outside the estimate
questions.why: A concrete risk in a partial service is illustrated in the direct costs of that service; overarching site risks go into construction site overheads; company-level costs such as the risk management system itself sit in general business expenses. What you could not identify is left to the venture and profit surcharge — which is why eroding that surcharge in a price war removes the buffer for the unknown.

questions.q: Build up the bid from the bottom. Put the cost blocks in order.
items: Direct cost of partial services (per specification position and cost element)
General business expenses (general, blanket as a percentage)
Risk and profit (general, blanket as a percentage)
questions.why: Direct costs plus site overheads make the production costs; adding general business expenses gives the prime cost; adding risk and profit gives the net bid. Knowing this ladder is what lets you say where in the price a given risk has been covered.

questions.q: What does risk controlling at project level involve?
options: Monitoring how risks change in the different phases of a project
Recognising that project decisions create new risk situations whose individual risks must be identified, analyzed and managed
Accepting that risks not assessed as serious can suddenly become a threat to success
Periodic monitoring of the effectiveness of the treatment measures
Adaptation of coping measures when risk potentials change
Freezing the risk register after contract award to keep the baseline stable
questions.why: Risk controlling has two objects — monitoring the risks and monitoring the measures. Freezing the register is the opposite of the concept: the example given is checking whether adjusting the construction sequencing actually mitigated the schedule risk as intended.

questions.q: Which are among the ten principles of risk-conscious action?
options: We only accept controllable risks
We do not deviate from established processes
We only work within the scope of our competence
We only accept orders of appropriate size
We only work with efficient and reliable partners
We only work under contract
We do not allow ourselves to be blackmailed
We report risk-relevant events without delay
We accept any order that shows a positive margin
questions.why: Eight of the ten are listed here; the remaining two are commitment to the highest safety standards and ensuring personnel competence and capacity. Accepting any profitable order contradicts principles 5 and 4 directly — size and competence are gates that a positive margin does not open.

questions.q: The lecture ends the risk-map section with lottery odds — a 1 in 139,838,160 chance of the jackpot, over 98 % probability of winning nothing, and a payout rate of only about 50 %. What is the point?
options: Never forget the human factor — people systematically misjudge probabilities, which is why risk assessment must be structured rather than intuitive
Lotteries are a viable project financing instrument
Low-probability risks can safely be ignored
Probability theory does not apply to construction
questions.why: The comparison with the ~1 in 3 million chance of being struck by lightning makes the bias visible: people overrate spectacular, tiny probabilities and underrate mundane ones. That is exactly why registers, maps and simulations exist instead of gut feeling.

questions.q: How does the guest lecture define Technical Controlling?
options: The systematic planning, monitoring and control of technical project parameters — scope, quantities, construction processes — to ensure economic efficiency and the achievement of project objectives
The technical inspection of works for compliance with building codes
The accounting function that produces the monthly financial statements
The quality assurance department's audit of the site
questions.why: The essence is expressing all project-relevant technical processes in monetary terms. As the slide insists, it is not about reporting numbers but about understanding what is happening, identifying deviations early and actively steering the outcome.

questions.q: Which are core areas of responsibility of Technical Controlling?
options: Performance and quantity controlling
Construction process and schedule controlling
Cost control from the technical perspective
Risk monitoring
Change order management — claims, variations, compensation events
Payroll and personnel administration
questions.why: Five areas, with four stated objectives: early identification of deviations, transparency within the project, ensuring economic efficiency, and supporting site management in decision-making. Payroll belongs to administration, not controlling.

questions.q: Sort each characteristic into Technical Controlling or Commercial Controlling.
questions.why: Technical Controlling looks at the physical project and monetises it; Commercial Controlling looks at the money and the cash flow. In practice both work closely together and the boundaries often overlap — internationally the technical side is split across roles such as cost engineer, quantity surveyor, project controls manager and claims consultant.

questions.q: Internationally, the tasks of a German "Technical Controller" are usually spread across several roles. Which?
options: Cost engineer, quantity surveyor, project controls manager and claims consultant
Site manager, foreman and safety officer
Design manager, BIM coordinator and surveyor
Procurement manager and logistics manager
questions.why: Together these four cover what is often a single function in the German construction industry. The role is described as interdisciplinary, a communication bridge, and a support for holistic decision-making — which is why splitting it across four people creates coordination risk.

questions.q: Why is estimation called "the backbone of the project"?
options: It defines the cost structure, quantities, productivity and risk assessment — the reference system for the whole project
It links tendering, contracting and execution through consistent estimating principles
The tender phase carries the highest uncertainty but the maximum leverage
Around 80 % of flopped or failed projects originate in the tender phase
Once submitted, the estimate is never revisited
questions.why: The last option is the opposite of the message: estimation is not a one-time activity, it evolves across project phases. The tender phase is described as the point in time with maximum error risk — limited information, time pressure, assumptions instead of facts.

questions.q: Put the three estimates in the order in which they arise across the project life cycle.
items: Tender estimate — strategic and uncertainty-driven; pricing and risk positioning (pre-construction)
Contract estimate — the contractual reference point defining scope, cost and obligations (contract negotiation and award)
Work estimate — the operational planning and steering tool, continuously updated with real data (delivery)
questions.why: Each estimate hands over to the next through continuous solution and consistent data management. The chain is what makes deviations meaningful: without a solid understanding of the estimate there is no meaningful analysis and no informed decision.

questions.q: The guest lecture pairs estimation and technical controlling in a formula. What is it?
options: Estimation = reference system; Technical Controlling = steering mechanism
Estimation = steering mechanism; Technical Controlling = reference system
Both are reference systems used at different times
Both are reporting duties with no steering function
questions.why: You cannot steer without a reference point. That is why the steering loop starts by setting the reference point with the estimate, then checks reality, analyses deviations, steers the project, and checks and balances the estimate again.

questions.q: Profit and entrepreneurial venture (5 %) plus company overhead charges (10 %) equal 15 % of the contract value. What is the corresponding surcharge as a percentage of the total job cost?
options: 15 %, since the reference base does not matter
30 %, since the two surcharges compound
questions.why: The two percentages have different reference bases: 15 % of the contract value is 17.65 % of the total job cost, because the surcharge is contained in the value it is measured against. In the worked example, a job cost of 650,000 plus 76,471 overhead and 38,235 profit gives a tender sum of 764,706.

questions.q: Put the project steering loop in order — "you don't manage the past, you steer the future".
items: Set the reference point with your estimate
questions.why: It is a loop, not a line: the estimate is rebalanced after steering and becomes the reference for the next cycle. The one-sentence version at the end of the guest lecture: plan the work, measure reality, detect deviations, take action.

questions.q: Sort each item into a cost-related or a revenue-related driver of the project margin.
questions.why: Both sides move the margin in both directions — risks and opportunities on the cost side, approved and rejected claims on the revenue side. The key insight is that margin is not fixed but dynamic: it develops through the project, as the tender → award → M1 → M3 → M6 → M12 → close-out curve shows.

questions.q: Match each point on the margin development curve to what happens there.
pairs: Shifting of risk and revised payment terms
Mobilisation cost and site installation reviewed
Productivity below plan and material cost increases
Final cost and revenue adjustments, residual risks materializing
questions.why: The curve tells a story rather than a number: an early dip from productivity and material costs, a recovery through mitigation and approved change orders, and a final correction as residual risks materialize. Reading it as a trend rather than a snapshot is the whole point.

questions.q: A claim is technically valid, formally submitted and acknowledged by the client, but the negotiation power is unclear and contractual interpretations differ. What is the typical practical mistake at this level?
options: Treating it as "almost secured revenue" and assigning overly high probabilities, which systematically overestimates margin and distorts forecasts
Withdrawing the claim to preserve the relationship
Recording it at zero value until it is paid in full
Escalating immediately to arbitration
questions.why: Acknowledgement is not approval. Outcomes are often reduced amounts, delays and partial approvals, so this level becomes critical when many claims are stuck in it, conversion to the next level is slow, and negotiations drag on.

questions.q: A claim has been formally rejected by the client, the contractor does not accept the rejection, and escalation to dispute or arbitration is possible. How should it be treated?
options: As a high-risk expectation, not as reliable revenue — it is no secured revenue, though not definitely lost either
As probable revenue, kept "in the pipeline"
As secured revenue, since the contractor is legally right
As a cost, since the claim has failed
questions.why: The lecture's line is that disputed claims are not neutral. Treating them internally as "probable revenue" causes a significant distortion of the true project picture, because resolution typically takes a long time, high effort and has an uncertain probability of success.

questions.q: Match each criterion to how it distinguishes contractor's risk from client's risk.
questions.why: The distinction determines what you actually do: a risk inside your scope is mitigated operationally, a risk outside it is managed through contractual compliance — notices, records and claims. Misclassifying the second as the first means you absorb a cost you were entitled to recover.

questions.q: Risk exposure is probability (%) × amount (€), continuously updated. Which early warning signals does the guest lecture name?
options: Risks increasing over time
Risks becoming issues
Provisions (contingencies) being consumed early
The number of entries in the risk register falling
questions.why: The three signals are about movement, not level: a growing exposure, a risk that has materialised into an issue, and contingency burned faster than progress earned it. A shrinking register is not a warning signal in itself — it might simply mean risks were closed out.

questions.q: Sort each risk into the area the guest lecture assigns it to.
items: Constructability issues and unforeseen ground conditions
Unapproved change orders and claim rejection
Unfavorable contract clauses and payment delays
Productivity shortfalls and material price increases
Delay in critical activities and permitting issues
Lack of qualified personnel and communication failures
Regulatory changes, political risks and force majeure events
questions.why: Seven areas — note that commercial and cost risks are kept apart: commercial risks arise from the contract (claims, clauses, payment), cost risks from execution and markets (productivity, prices, subcontractors). Mixing them hides who can act on them.

questions.q: Which factors distort a clear project picture, according to the guest lecture?
options: Optimism bias / wishful thinking — overconfidence in productivity, "we will catch up later", ignoring early negative trends
Misclassifying facts as risks — known issues reported as "risks" although the cost impact is already incurred
Overstating revenue — unapproved change orders recognised as secured revenue
