Underreporting costs — delayed recognition of overruns, "smoothing" cost curves, deferring bad news
Snapshot thinking instead of trends — focusing on a single reporting date
Incomplete scope visibility — missing quantities, hidden scope growth, interfaces not fully captured
Lack of integration (silos) — cost, schedule and risk not aligned, different "versions of truth"
Using a single integrated data source for cost, schedule and risk
questions.why: Seven distortions, each with its own consequence: problems recognised too late, delayed recognition of real impact, artificially inflated margin, a margin that appears stable then suddenly collapses, missed early warning signals, systematic underestimation of total cost, and wrong conclusions despite correct data. A single integrated data source is the cure for the seventh, not a distortion.

questions.q: In a plan-versus-actual comparison of cost, productivity and progress, which question does the guest lecture insist you ask about every deviation?
options: Single event or trend?
Who is to blame?
Can it be hidden until the next reporting date?
Does it exceed the contingency?
questions.why: A one-off deviation and the first point of a trend look identical in a single reporting period — which is exactly what snapshot thinking gets wrong. Distinguishing them decides whether you note it or act on it, since project failures are not sudden but develop over time.

questions.q: What principle governs structured change order management in the guest lecture?
options: Not all revenue is equal — the level of certainty must be transparent, and activation of revenue must follow clear regulations and principles
All submitted change orders should be recognised immediately to keep the forecast optimistic
Change orders should only be recorded once cash has been received
Change orders are a legal matter and do not belong in controlling
questions.why: The levels of a claim — submitted, acknowledged, rejected, approved — carry very different certainties, and the register must show which. Recognising everything early inflates the margin; recognising nothing until payment destroys the steering value of the forecast.

questions.q: Recall the key takeaways of the Technical Controlling guest lecture.
questions.answer:
• Estimation is the backbone — it defines the reference point across all project phases.
  • Project steering bridges plan and reality — by continuously monitoring and adjusting performance.
  • Margin is not fixed, it is dynamic — influenced by cost, revenue and risk events.
  • Early warning is critical — project failures are not sudden, they develop over time.
  • Transparency can be distorted — data must be interpreted critically, not blindly trusted.

Technical Controlling in one sentence: Plan the work. Measure reality. Detect deviations. Take action.
questions.why: Guest lectures are explicitly exam-relevant, and these five takeaways are the lecture's own summary.

questions.q: Recall the "You should know" list of Lecture 6.
questions.answer:
• Risk definition
  • Risk types in project management
  • Strategies for avoiding, assessing and managing risks
  • Causes and impacts of risks in a project
questions.why: This is the stated exam scope for Lecture 6; the Technical Controlling guest lecture is exam-relevant on top of it.

questions.q: Which practical tips and mindset qualities does the career guest lecture give to career starters?
options: Networking
Learning from feedback
Self-reflection
Time management
Patience, initiative, resilience and curiosity
Avoiding assignments abroad until you are senior
questions.why: Four practical tips and four mindset qualities. The lecture argues the opposite of the last option — early international experience is exactly what develops the flexibility, diplomacy and cross-cultural leadership that senior roles require.

questions.q: Which consequences of the language barrier does the career guest lecture report from practice in the UAE?
options: Incorrect execution of instructions due to misunderstanding of technical terms
Delays because messages must be repeated or clarified several times
Difficulty expressing complex ideas or feedback, especially under pressure
Frustration or tension among colleagues after repeated misunderstandings
Hesitation to speak up in meetings for fear of making mistakes
A reduction in the number of nationalities on site
questions.why: Five concrete effects, and note that the first two are cost and schedule impacts, not soft issues. This is the practical evidence for Lecture 3's figures on decision-making taking over 50 % longer in international teams.

questions.q: Which differences in working styles and communication does the career guest lecture name?
options: Different approaches to time — punctuality versus flexibility, planning versus improvising
Decision-making styles — top-down versus consensus-oriented, speed versus caution
Attitude toward conflict — confrontation versus avoidance
Work-life balance — "always on" culture versus strict work boundaries
Direct versus indirect communication, and verbal versus nonverbal cues
Initiative versus obedience, and flat versus formal structures
Uniform technical vocabulary shared by all nationalities on site
questions.why: These axes are the practitioner's version of Lecture 3's theory — Hofstede's power distance shows up as initiative versus obedience, Lewis's types as direct versus indirect communication. The reported benefits are cultural awareness, stronger team collaboration, diverse perspectives and personal development.

questions.q: Which site-management topic is specific to construction in the Gulf region and is managed via a "thermal working limit"?
options: Heat stress management
Frost protection of concrete
Flood defence of the site
Noise emission limits at night
questions.why: Heat stress management follows the ADOSH-SF technical guideline "Safety in the Heat". It sits alongside worker's welfare, safety and health, and regional conflict as the health-and-safety realities of construction in the UAE.

questions.q: The Thiba Dam in Kenya (€73 m, completed 09.2022, financed by a JICA loan) is used to answer the question of how host-country populations react to a foreign-led project. What did the project deliver locally?
options: Allowing for two annual rice harvests
A stable supply of irrigation water
Recruitment and training of a workforce of about 600 workers from surrounding local communities
Internships for local engineers
Support of the local population and local aid organizations
Full transfer of dam ownership to the contractor
questions.why: Acceptance was earned through local benefit — harvests, water, jobs, training and community support. Contrast it with Mtentu in Lecture 1, where broken promises of employment led to protests, threats and termination: the same stakeholder logic with the opposite outcome.

questions.q: The lecture claims that financing major projects can influence world politics and history. Which example does it use?
options: St. Peter's Basilica — the sale of indulgences to finance construction was one of the main triggers of the Reformation
The Suez Canal and the Franco-British rivalry
The Berlin Brandenburg Airport and German federal politics
The Channel Tunnel and British EU membership
questions.why: Construction began in 1506 and finished in 1626; the enormous costs were funded partly through indulgences, and Luther's 95 Theses of 1517 attacked exactly that practice. The lesson for the course: how you finance a project is never a purely technical decision.

questions.q: Why is working on international construction sites interesting, according to the closing recapitulation?
options: Cultural aspects — insight into different cultures, languages and traditions, and how culture influences design, materials and methods
Variety of projects — large-scale, high-profile works with unique environmental, regulatory and logistical challenges
Technical challenges — different engineering standards, climates, seismic zones and local materials
Professional growth — an enhanced CV, multi-national teamwork, soft skills such as flexibility and diplomacy
Adventure and travel
Higher earning potential — tax exemptions, relocation bonuses, housing and car, especially in remote or high-demand regions
Shorter working hours and lighter workload than on domestic sites
questions.why: Six reasons are listed — an easier workload is emphatically not one of them. They form the mirror image of the course's risk catalogue: nearly every factor that makes international work risky — cultural distance, unfamiliar standards, remote locations — is also what makes it professionally valuable.
